stem: An enterprise runs a generative AI (GenAI) document summarization workload in a dedicated application AWS account using Amazon Bedrock. The architecture consists of an Amazon API Gateway REST API that routes requests to AWS Lambda functions deployed within private VPC subnets. The workload processes confidential customer records stored in a governed data lake hosted in a separate, centralized AWS data storage account that has Amazon S3, Amazon Athena, and AWS Glue enabled. All Bedrock API calls from the application must travel exclusively over private network paths without traversing the public internet. The governed data lake must enforce fine-grained column-level access controls that apply consistently across both AWS accounts. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Deploy Lambda functions in private subnets. Attach a NAT Gateway to the VPC to route outbound traffic to Bedrock and the data lake. Manage data lake permissions using S3 bucket policies and ACLs. Export AWS CloudTrail logs to S3 for weekly manual review.
options.rationale: because a NAT Gateway only routes traffic through the public internet, directly violating the requirement for private-only connectivity to Amazon Bedrock. S3 bucket policies and ACLs also cannot enforce column-level access controls; they operate only at the object and bucket levels, making them unsuitable for fine-grained data lake governance.

options.text: Provision a gateway VPC endpoint for S3 only in the application account. Allow Lambda functions to invoke Bedrock through public internet endpoints. Use database-level grants in AWS Lake Formation to control data access. Forward AWS CloudTrail logs to Amazon CloudWatch Logs without configuring metric filters or alerting.
options.rationale: because Amazon Bedrock is simply not supported by gateway endpoints; it requires interface VPC endpoints for private connectivity. Invoking Bedrock through public endpoints directly violates the private connectivity requirement. Database-level Lake Formation grants also do not satisfy the column-level access control requirement.

options.text: In the application account, provision interface VPC endpoints for Bedrock runtime APIs. Deploy Lambda functions within private subnets. Apply IAM condition keys on inference and data-plane policies to restrict calls to approved endpoints and authorized roles only. In the data storage account, configure AWS Lake Formation LF-tag-based access control to establish table-level and column-level cross-account permission grants.

Create VPC endpoints for both Bedrock and S3 in the application account. Rely exclusively on IAM path-based policies to govern data lake access. Publish AWS CloudTrail logs to Amazon CloudWatch Logs. Permit public endpoint fallback for cross-Region reads to simplify cross-account configuration.
options.rationale: because while VPC endpoints are correctly provisioned, allowing public endpoint fallback reintroduces internet-bound traffic and violates the private connectivity requirement. IAM path-based policies alone also cannot enforce column-level data lake access; AWS Lake Formation with LF-tag-based access control is required for that level of granularity across accounts.

correct_text: In the application account, provision interface VPC endpoints for Bedrock runtime APIs. Deploy Lambda functions within private subnets. Apply IAM condition keys on inference and data-plane policies to restrict calls to approved endpoints and authorized roles only. In the data storage account, configure AWS Lake Formation LF-tag-based access control to establish table-level and column-level cross-account permission grants.
concepto: Bedrock VPC endpoints + Lake Formation LF-tags

stem: A financial services organization is developing a generative AI (GenAI) application that generates insights from multiple datasets by combining information retrieved from Amazon S3 and third-party SaaS platforms integrated using Amazon AppFlow within a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) workflow. The application requires a centralized registry to manage registered data sources and must apply metadata tagging to link generated outputs back to the originating datasets. The system must preserve end-to-end data lineage across all processing stages. All data access and system activity must also be immutably logged to support compliance and auditing requirements. Which solution provides the most appropriate architecture for these requirements?

options.text: Integrate Amazon Macie to scan and classify the research reports and trading logs. Use AWS CloudTrail to log all API requests and data access events.
options.rationale: because Amazon Macie is primarily used for sensitive data discovery and classification. It simply generates findings and sensitivity scores based on detected data patterns. While it can analyze data in Amazon S3, it does not provide a centralized metadata registry or support custom metadata tagging for data lineage and source attribution.

options.text: Create a unified registry using the AWS Glue Data Catalog and apply custom tags for data lineage. Send all pipeline execution logs and access events to Amazon CloudWatch Logs for compliance tracking.
options.rationale: because Amazon CloudWatch Logs just collects application and system logs but does not provide authoritative, immutable audit logs across AWS services. It simply lacks the API-level audit capability required for compliance, which is only provided by AWS CloudTrail.

options.text: Use AWS Lake Formation to manage fine-grained access control and permissions for the datasets. Use Amazon CloudWatch Logs to collect application logs and monitor access patterns.
options.rationale: because AWS Lake Formation focuses on data lake permissions and governance rather than acting as a centralized metadata registry for attribution. Additionally, Amazon CloudWatch Logs only captures application-level logs and does not provide the cross-service, immutable audit trail required for compliance.

options.text: Provision the AWS Glue Data Catalog for data source registration and apply metadata tags to attribute content. Enable AWS CloudTrail to immutably log API activity and data access events across the architecture.

correct_text: Provision the AWS Glue Data Catalog for data source registration and apply metadata tags to attribute content. Enable AWS CloudTrail to immutably log API activity and data access events across the architecture.
concepto: Glue Data Catalog + CloudTrail para lineage GenAI

category: AIP – Implementation and Integration
stem: A retail company is integrating Amazon Bedrock into an existing e-commerce platform to power a generative AI (GenAI) application. To automate product listing creation, the team designed a multi-agent workflow using AWS Step Functions. Three agents run in sequence: a content creator, a technical validator, and a brand alignment reviewer, each building on the reasoning traces and outputs of the previous agent. All processing artifacts and final outputs are stored in an Amazon S3 bucket. During a testing phase, the team begins seeing consistent workflow failures. Investigation reveals that intermediate payloads passed between states regularly exceed the 256 KB Step Functions quota, halting execution before completion. To address this, a GenAI Engineer is tasked with reworking the architecture so that large payloads no longer trigger execution failures. The solution must also retain end-to-end workflow observability and maintain the multi-agent reasoning and acting (ReAct) pattern. Which of the following architectural modifications fulfills these specifications while minimizing operational overhead?

options.text: Store the extensive reasoning logs in an Amazon DynamoDB table, passing only the partition keys through the execution flow. Introduce a Map state to dynamically query DynamoDB and fetch the full text payloads immediately before each agent executes its assigned task.
options.rationale: because simply introducing Amazon DynamoDB adds unnecessary architectural complexity and cost when Amazon S3 is already configured to store processing artifacts. Additionally, a Map state is primarily designed for parallel processing of array items, making it architecturally inappropriate for a sequential, multi-agent validation pipeline.

options.text: Update the optimized Bedrock API calls to ingest large payloads directly from a S3 URI. Extract the newly generated S3 object locations using ResultSelector and append these lightweight pointers to the state payload using ResultPath, enabling the seamless chaining of agents without breaching payload quotas.

Deploy an Amazon ElastiCache for Redis cluster to temporarily cache the reasoning logs. Update the state machine to use Task states that write the large payloads to Redis and pass only the cache keys to the next agent, ensuring the payload remains under 256 KB.
options.rationale: because provisioning and maintaining an Amazon ElastiCache cluster introduces massive operational overhead. The engineering team would need to manage VPC networking, cluster maintenance, and write custom integration code, which violates the requirement for the least operational burden.

options.text: Transition the orchestration layer from Step Functions to Amazon Managed Workflows for Apache Airflow (Amazon MWAA). Construct a directed acyclic graph (DAG) where XComs are configured with a custom S3 backend to pass the massive payload data between the different agent tasks.
options.rationale: because migrating the entire orchestration layer to MWAA requires completely rewriting the application logic. This represents a drastic architectural pivot that just introduces significant ongoing infrastructure management and completely fails the requirement to minimize operational overhead.

correct_text: Update the optimized Bedrock API calls to ingest large payloads directly from a S3 URI. Extract the newly generated S3 object locations using ResultSelector and append these lightweight pointers to the state payload using ResultPath, enabling the seamless chaining of agents without breaching payload quotas.
concepto: Step Functions payload S3 URI ResultPath para agentes GenAI

category: AIP – AI Safety, Security, and Governance
stem: A GenAI developer maintains a customer-facing assistant powered by a foundation model (FM) in Amazon Bedrock. During routine evaluations, the developer notices that the assistant occasionally produces different answers for prompts that have only minor wording differences. To investigate this behavior, the developer assembles a structured prompt dataset containing several closely related variants of each query and configures Amazon SNS to receive notifications whenever new evaluation batches are initiated. The goal is to run a quantitative robustness analysis to determine how sensitive the FM is to these small variations and to measure the consistency of its generated responses. Which solution will quantitatively evaluate the model’s output across these closely related prompt variations?

options.text: Select an Anthropic Claude model running in Bedrock at temperature 0, then run an AWS Lambda script that applies Levenshtein distance to determine how dissimilar the responses.
options.rationale: because a zero-temperature setting reduces randomness, but Levenshtein distance only compares literal string differences and does not measure reasoning consistency or semantic robustness. Two responses may differ slightly in text but convey identical meaning, or appear similar but diverge conceptually. This fails to provide a true robustness evaluation.

options.text: Launch a Bedrock model evaluation job using the prepared prompt dataset and enable robustness metrics to analyze statistical differences in responses across similar prompts.

Use Bedrock Pipelines to run batch inference on the grouped prompts and store all responses in Amazon S3. Process the outputs with Amazon Comprehend to compute linguistic similarity scores and compare variations across related prompts.
options.rationale: because Bedrock Pipelines and Comprehend can help batch process text and compute linguistic similarity, but they do not offer built-in robustness scoring or statistical evaluation. This becomes a custom pipeline with no standardized robustness metric, making it ineffective for quantitative output-stability analysis.

options.text: Create an automated workflow using AWS Step Functions that repeatedly invokes the FM with randomized system prompts. Aggregate all responses and use custom logic to evaluate how much the model’s outputs diverge across each prompt variation.
options.rationale: because Step Functions can typically automate repeated FM invocations, but this still requires fully custom logic to measure variance or consistency. It does not provide native robustness metrics, statistical scoring, or evaluation tooling. It introduces additional operational complexity without delivering the required quantitative evaluation.

correct_text: Launch a Bedrock model evaluation job using the prepared prompt dataset and enable robustness metrics to analyze statistical differences in responses across similar prompts.
concepto: Bedrock model evaluation robustness metrics

category: AIP – Foundation Model Integration, Data Management, and Compliance
stem: A digital publishing company is building a content creation platform that allows contributors to upload article drafts and supporting images. The platform uses Amazon Bedrock to transform the submitted material into summaries, promotional copy, and visual content descriptions. All uploaded files enter the application through an existing Amazon S3 storage workflow. Before any content is processed or published, the company must detect and remove personally identifiable information (PII) from submitted text, identify inappropriate or unsafe images, and prevent Bedrock from accepting or generating harmful content. The company wants to coordinate these checks automatically while minimizing the amount of infrastructure it must operate. Which approach will meet these requirements while minimizing infrastructure management?

options.text: Orchestrate the moderation process with AWS Step Functions. Use Amazon Comprehend to detect and redact PII from submitted text, apply Amazon Rekognition moderation checks to uploaded images, and enforce Bedrock Guardrails on model inputs and outputs before the content proceeds through the workflow.

Trigger AWS Lambda when new content is uploaded to S3. Use Amazon Comprehend to detect PII and Amazon Rekognition to moderate images, then implement custom Lambda filtering rules for Bedrock inputs and generated outputs.
options.rationale: because the custom Lambda filtering logic would primarily duplicate functionality already provided by Amazon Bedrock Guardrails. The company would also need to develop, test, update, and maintain its own rules for controlling harmful model inputs and outputs instead of using configurable managed safeguards.

options.text: Use Amazon EventBridge to route S3 upload events to separate AWS Lambda functions. Have one function call Amazon Comprehend for PII detection, another call Amazon Rekognition for image moderation, and a third invoke Bedrock after all moderation checks complete.
options.rationale: because this architecture would typically require additional custom coordination to track whether each independent moderation step completed successfully and whether the content is safe to continue processing. It also omits Amazon Bedrock Guardrails, so the foundation model’s own inputs and outputs do not receive the required managed harmful-content filtering.

options.text: Deploy an Amazon ECS service to process files uploaded to S3. Use Amazon Comprehend to inspect text for PII, Amazon Rekognition to identify inappropriate images, and custom application logic to validate content before and after invoking Bedrock.
options.rationale: because running an ECS-based moderation application would simply introduce more infrastructure and custom code to deploy, scale, monitor, and maintain. It also substitutes custom Bedrock validation logic for the managed filtering capabilities available through Amazon Bedrock Guardrails.

correct_text: Orchestrate the moderation process with AWS Step Functions. Use Amazon Comprehend to detect and redact PII from submitted text, apply Amazon Rekognition moderation checks to uploaded images, and enforce Bedrock Guardrails on model inputs and outputs before the content proceeds through the workflow.
concepto: Comprehend PII + Rekognition moderation + Bedrock Guardrails

stem: A company operates a global e-learning marketplace that helps learners discover courses and instructors. The platform has 40 million monthly active users and manages a catalog of 15 million courses and 150 million learner reviews currently stored in a PostgreSQL database. The company wants to implement a semantic search solution that lets learners find courses via natural-language queries such as “beginner-friendly machine learning course with project-based labs.” The solution must handle complex natural-language queries and return results for at least 95% of queries within 500 milliseconds. The company also wants to continuously validate the application’s end-to-end search experience and response latency using Amazon CloudWatch Synthetics canaries. Course details and ratings are updated hourly, and the index must reflect those updates. The solution must also scale cost-effectively during peak enrollment periods. Which solution satisfies these requirements with the lowest development effort?

options.text: Connect the course catalog data to an Amazon Kendra index. Use Kendra's NLP-based retrieval to handle natural language learner queries. Schedule hourly Kendra data source sync jobs to keep course details and ratings current. Expose results through an Amazon API Gateway endpoint.
options.rationale: because Amazon Kendra is just optimized for enterprise document retrieval workloads and does not expose raw vector search capabilities at the scale of 150 million reviews. Its pricing model and concurrency characteristics are not cost-effective for a consumer-facing discovery platform with 40 million monthly active users under peak load.

options.text: Migrate the course catalog to Amazon OpenSearch Service. Use a foundation model in Amazon Bedrock to generate vector embeddings from course descriptions, syllabi, and reviews. At query time, convert natural language inputs to embeddings using the same model. Perform k-NN searches against the OpenSearch vector index to return semantically similar results.
options.rationale: . While Amazon OpenSearch Service with Bedrock embeddings can meet the performance requirements, it primarily requires a custom embedding pipeline, hourly re-ingestion logic, query-time embedding orchestration, and index tuning, all of which entail substantial development effort that the managed Bedrock Knowledge Base eliminates.

options.text: Migrate the course catalog to Amazon Neptune Analytics. Configure a vector index in Neptune Analytics to store embeddings generated from course and review data using a foundation model in Amazon Bedrock. Write AWS Lambda functions to handle query-time embedding generation and execute vector similarity searches against the Neptune Analytics graph index.
options.rationale: because using Amazon Neptune Analytics as a standalone vector store with custom Lambda functions requires building the same embedding pipeline, query-time orchestration, and hourly refresh logic that the managed Bedrock Knowledge Base handles automatically, only producing a higher development and maintenance burden for no additional semantic search benefit at this scale.

options.text: Load the course catalog into an Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base using a scheduled ingestion pipeline. Configure the knowledge base to automatically generate and store embeddings during ingestion. Use the Bedrock Retrieve API, with built-in vector search capabilities, to query the knowledge base directly from natural-language learner input, without building custom query-time embedding or retrieval logic.

correct_text: Load the course catalog into an Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base using a scheduled ingestion pipeline. Configure the knowledge base to automatically generate and store embeddings during ingestion. Use the Bedrock Retrieve API, with built-in vector search capabilities, to query the knowledge base directly from natural-language learner input, without building custom query-time embedding or retrieval logic.
concepto: Bedrock Knowledge Base semantic search + Retrieve API

category: AIP – AI Safety, Security, and Governance
stem: A research group operates TD Owl, a secure analytics platform that processes highly confidential regulatory documents, internal valuation reports, and sensitive liquidity forecasts. As part of a new analytical initiative, the organization incorporated foundation model (FM) capabilities to derive structured insights from sensitive financial content. The environment already uses Amazon SageMaker Feature Store to manage feature vectors and Amazon Textract to extract critical fields from regulated documents, but a security review revealed concerns about how FM interactions handle confidential material. The assessment noted that certain FM-generated outputs include references to internal identifiers that must not persist beyond a single inference request due to strict confidentiality mandates. Regulatory requirements prohibit retaining prompts, storing outputs, or allowing sensitive financial data to influence future FM behavior. To meet compliance standards, the architecture team must implement an approach that ensures FM interactions remain fully isolated, prevents any form of data retention, and relies on managed AWS capabilities that inherently protect sensitive inputs and outputs without requiring custom-built sanitization systems. Which solution BEST meets this requirement for securing foundation model interactions?

options.text: Enable AWS CloudTrail data event logging to record FM invocation activity and capture operational metadata that supports compliance monitoring while preventing the collection of full prompt or output content.
options.rationale: because CloudTrail logs are typically designed to retain detailed event records for auditing and security analysis, which introduces ongoing storage and potential exposure of sensitive interaction metadata instead of enforcing strict non-retention of FM activity. This approach focuses on observability and traceability rather than providing the isolated, non-persistent processing model required for foundation model interactions involving highly confidential data.

options.text: Use AWS Key Management Service (KMS) to encrypt all FM prompts and outputs in Amazon S3, with automatic lifecycle policies to delete data shortly after processing.
options.rationale: because KMS and S3 lifecycle configurations primarily protect data at rest and control when stored objects are deleted, but the design still persists sensitive prompts and outputs for a period of time instead of eliminating storage entirely. This pattern does not align with a privacy model where FM interactions must be ephemeral and must avoid any intermediate retention of confidential information, even in encrypted form.

options.text: Implement an AWS Lambda preprocessing step to mask sensitive identifiers before sending data to the FM, then store masked outputs for limited audit review.
options.rationale: because masking and partial storage just reduce the direct identifiability of the data, while still keeping derived content that can remain sensitive and subject to governance. This pattern continues to create an audit repository and preserves FM outputs, which conflicts with a requirement that calls for fully isolated interactions and the complete avoidance of storing prompts or responses.

options.text: Employ Amazon Bedrock native data privacy features to prevent prompt and output retention, and ensure isolated foundation model interactions.

correct_text: Employ Amazon Bedrock native data privacy features to prevent prompt and output retention, and ensure isolated foundation model interactions.
concepto: Bedrock native data privacy (no retention)

stem: A multinational healthcare provider is building an AI agent using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime to help care coordinators answer patient questions, schedule follow‑ups, and explain coverage terms. The organization wants to enforce its corporate SSO via an OpenID Connect (OIDC) identity provider (IdP) so that only authenticated staff can use the agent. The system also runs Amazon SageMaker AI to generate personalized health plan summaries and Amazon Translate to support multi-language responses for global users. To secure the agent, Bedrock AgentCore must only accept inbound tokens from the IdP when the token’s audience matches the specific application ID. At the same time, the maximum tokens parameter should be optimized to control the length of agent responses and reduce downstream generation costs. Which configuration should be used?

options.text: Use IAM-only authentication for AgentCore Runtime and validate requests with SigV4 without using OIDC.
options.rationale: . This option primarily relies on AWS IAM credentials, which only authenticate AWS API calls. It does not validate user identities through the corporate IdP or enforce audience restrictions for the specific application. As a result, it simply cannot guarantee that only authorized staff can access the AI agent. While IAM provides coarse-grained access control, it is typically insufficient for scenarios requiring strict user authentication and SSO integration.

options.text: Link AgentCore Identity to the IdP for outbound authentication only, so the agent uses the IdP to request tokens but does not enforce inbound OIDC validation.
options.rationale: . This approach allows the agent to request tokens for accessing external services but does not enforce inbound token validation. It is primarily intended for agent-to-service authentication, not for restricting which users can invoke the agent. Using outbound-only authentication simply fails to provide the necessary access control for sensitive patient or corporate data. Consequently, it is only suitable for securing outgoing API calls and cannot replace inbound identity verification.

options.text: Configure AgentCore Identity as an inbound provider via OIDC. Set allowed audiences to the corporate application ID, and tune the maximum tokens parameter for generation.
Set up Amazon Cognito user pools as an inbound identity provider for AgentCore, map the IdP application ID as an allowed audience, and set the maximum tokens to control the response length.
options.rationale: . While Cognito can enforce inbound identity validation, it adds an extra layer of complexity when the organization already has a corporate IdP supporting OIDC. This method is typically more complex than directly configuring AgentCore Identity as an inbound OIDC provider. It may also introduce additional maintenance overhead and latency.

correct_text: Configure AgentCore Identity as an inbound provider via OIDC. Set allowed audiences to the corporate application ID, and tune the maximum tokens parameter for generation.
concepto: Bedrock AgentCore Identity OIDC inbound provider

category: AIP – Implementation and Integration
stem: A finance company is deploying a Generative AI research tool to assist portfolio managers with market data analysis. It must deliver insights in under 1.5 seconds and handle up to 500 simultaneous analytical requests during market open. The application should address multi-part financial inquiries by referencing internal Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) filings and earnings reports, accurately break down these prompts, and avoid semantic dilution to achieve high accuracy. Which solution satisfies these requirements while minimizing operational complexity?

options.text: Provision an Amazon OpenSearch Serverless collection to store vector embeddings of the financial documents. Write custom AWS Lambda functions to parse and split user prompts before sending the requests to an Amazon Bedrock foundation model.
options.rationale: because manually building and maintaining AWS Lambda functions just to handle query decomposition adds unnecessary architectural complexity and administrative burden compared to using the native query decomposition feature in Amazon Bedrock.

options.text: Configure an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base as the repository for the SEC filings and earnings reports and toggle on the query decomposition feature. To power the application, implement a Bedrock flow that integrates the knowledge base with a foundation model.

Train custom natural language processing (NLP) models on Amazon SageMaker AI to perform query parsing and expansion. Securely store the financial documents in an encrypted Amazon Bedrock knowledge base.
options.rationale: because developing, training, and hosting custom machine learning models on Amazon SageMaker AI introduces significant operational overhead. A fully managed approach using native features in Amazon Bedrock is far more efficient for this use case.

options.text: Create an Amazon Kendra index to ingest the financial reports and enable natural language search. Utilize an Amazon Bedrock agent equipped with advanced reasoning to orchestrate the step-by-step query decomposition process.
options.rationale: because while Amazon Kendra is a powerful search service, using an Amazon Bedrock agent to orchestrate complex reasoning and decomposition steps involves more configuration and overhead than only enabling the built-in decomposition feature of an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base and flow.

correct_text: Configure an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base as the repository for the SEC filings and earnings reports and toggle on the query decomposition feature. To power the application, implement a Bedrock flow that integrates the knowledge base with a foundation model.
concepto: Bedrock Knowledge Base query decomposition + flows

stem: A manufacturing company uses Amazon Bedrock to power a Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) assistant for maintenance engineers. The Bedrock knowledge base uses an Amazon S3 bucket as its data source, containing equipment manuals, inspection reports, repair logs, and safety procedures collected across multiple factories and equipment models. The current semantic search frequently evaluates documents for unrelated facilities, machine types, and maintenance periods, which reduces retrieval accuracy and increases the amount of irrelevant content returned to the application. Each document already has descriptive attributes such as facility, equipment category, model number, document type, and revision date. The company wants to use these attributes to narrow retrieval results without replacing the existing embedding model or redesigning the knowledge base. Which solution will improve retrieval relevance with the fewest changes to the existing architecture?

options.text: Enable a reranking model in the Bedrock Knowledge Base to reorder retrieved chunks based on semantic relevance. Increase the number of retrieved results so the application has more candidate documents to evaluate before generating a response.
options.rationale: because reranking primarily reorders chunks that have already been retrieved according to their relevance to the query. Although reranking can improve result quality, it does not directly use the existing facility, model, document-type, and date attributes to constrain which documents qualify for retrieval. Increasing the number of candidate results can also cause more content to be evaluated instead of directly narrowing the search space with metadata filters.

options.text: Ingest the S3 document metadata into the Bedrock Knowledge Base by using associated metadata files, and apply metadata-aware filtering to restrict searches to documents that match the relevant attributes.

Enable query decomposition in the Bedrock Knowledge Base so complex user questions are divided into smaller subqueries. Run each subquery across the complete S3 data source and combine the retrieved results before generation.
options.rationale: because query decomposition typically improves retrieval for multifaceted questions by dividing them into smaller queries. It does not inherently restrict those queries to the correct factory, equipment model, document category, or revision period. Without metadata filters, the resulting subqueries can still retrieve content from unrelated portions of the knowledge base.

options.text: Rebuild the S3 documents with smaller text chunks and resynchronize the Bedrock Knowledge Base. Keep the existing vector search configuration and rely on the embedding model to identify the most relevant content across all facilities, equipment types, and dates.
options.rationale: because changing the chunking strategy would simply alter how individual documents are divided during ingestion. Smaller chunks may change retrieval granularity, but they do not prevent the retrieval system from considering documents from irrelevant facilities, equipment categories, or time ranges. The problem is better addressed by filtering on the metadata attributes that already identify those distinctions.

correct_text: Ingest the S3 document metadata into the Bedrock Knowledge Base by using associated metadata files, and apply metadata-aware filtering to restrict searches to documents that match the relevant attributes.
concepto: Bedrock Knowledge Base metadata filtering

stem: An insurance company is building a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) assistant that uses Amazon Bedrock foundation models to help claims specialists search historical customer interactions and policy-support records. Approximately 60 GB of archived claim conversations are stored in an Amazon S3 bucket as JSON files, and the company plans to use the processed content as its retrieval corpus. Before the records can be indexed, the processing workflow must identify and remove personally identifiable information (PII), generate embeddings for vector storage, and make the resulting vectors available for low-latency similarity searches. The company wants a managed workflow that can coordinate these processing stages and minimize the amount of custom infrastructure required. Which approach will meet these requirements while minimizing operational effort?

options.text: Use AWS Lambda functions triggered by S3 events to parse the JSON files, call Amazon Comprehend for PII detection, and invoke Bedrock to generate embeddings. Store the vectors in Amazon DynamoDB and implement custom similarity-scoring logic in Lambda.
options.rationale: because this approach would primarily require custom code to coordinate processing and perform vector similarity calculations. Amazon OpenSearch Serverless already provides purpose-built vector indexing and k-NN similarity search, so implementing those capabilities manually increases development and operational effort.

options.text: Use AWS Glue ETL jobs to process the JSON files from S3, remove PII with custom transformation code, and invoke Bedrock to generate embeddings. Write the embeddings back to S3 and use Amazon Athena queries to identify similar records.
options.rationale: because Amazon S3 and Athena are typically used for durable object storage and analytical SQL queries rather than low-latency vector similarity retrieval. Simply storing embedding arrays in S3 does not provide the vector index and k-NN search capabilities that the RAG application requires.

options.text: Use AWS Step Functions to coordinate the data-preparation pipeline. Have Amazon Comprehend identify PII in the source content, pass the sanitized text to Bedrock to create embeddings, and write the resulting vectors directly to Amazon OpenSearch Serverless for storage and similarity-based retrieval.

Use Amazon EMR Serverless to process the historical conversations with Apache Spark, call Amazon Comprehend for PII detection, and generate embeddings with Bedrock. Load the resulting vectors into a self-managed OpenSearch domain and maintain the indexing and scaling configuration manually.
options.rationale: because this architecture would simply add unnecessary processing and search-infrastructure management. Amazon EMR Serverless can perform large-scale data processing, but the scenario does not require a custom Spark processing framework, while a self-managed OpenSearch configuration introduces additional scaling and administration compared with OpenSearch Serverless.

correct_text: Use AWS Step Functions to coordinate the data-preparation pipeline. Have Amazon Comprehend identify PII in the source content, pass the sanitized text to Bedrock to create embeddings, and write the resulting vectors directly to Amazon OpenSearch Serverless for storage and similarity-based retrieval.
concepto: Comprehend PII + Bedrock embeddings + OpenSearch Serverless

category: AIP – Implementation and Integration
stem: A research organization is building an automated knowledge pipeline for its TDiscover platform. Each incoming dataset is first processed by Amazon Rekognition to extract visual details that help guide downstream analysis. After this initial step, the workflow sends a request to a foundation model (FM) in Amazon Bedrock so the system can generate structured insights and interpret the extracted information. The development team wants the FM to follow a clear reasoning pattern by breaking each task into a sequence of logical steps. The evaluation process includes reviewing different workflow designs and considering the use of AWS Step Functions to reliably coordinate each stage, validate transitions, and ensure all reasoning steps are performed in a consistent manner. Which approach will deliver this structured reasoning behavior in the most reliable manner?

options.text: Build a Step Functions state machine that embeds every reasoning instruction into a single state. Provide one combined prompt to the FM and depend on a single model invocation to produce the complete reasoning output without breaking it into validated steps.
options.rationale: because combining all reasoning instructions into one state typically eliminates the structured coordination that Step Functions is designed to provide. Without dividing the reasoning into multiple controlled states, the system loses the ability to validate intermediate outputs, adjust the flow, or recover from partial failures. This results in a single, consolidated FM call that lacks the consistent, step-by-step reasoning process required by the scenario.

options.text: Build a Step Functions state machine that uses a Parallel state to evaluate multiple possible reasoning directions. After collecting all FM outputs, use a final Task state to let the model select the most suitable reasoning path from the combined results.
options.rationale: because Parallel states are primarily designed for executing branches that do not depend on each other’s intermediate reasoning. Even though the workflow collects all FM responses at the end and uses a final Task state to choose the preferred path, the reasoning phases still run in isolation without shared context. Each branch works with its own partial understanding rather than building on prior steps, which prevents the model from following a unified, sequential reasoning process. This leads to fragmented outputs across branches and makes it impossible to maintain the consistent, step-by-step reasoning flow required in the scenario.

options.text: Build a Step Functions state machine that guides the FM through a chain-of-thought sequence, using predefined prompt templates. Add Choice states to shift the reasoning route based on intermediate model outputs.
options.rationale: because chain-of-thought prompting only works predictably when the reasoning path remains stable from start to finish. Introducing Choice states that alter the flow based on intermediate model responses creates unpredictable branching and allows the FM to diverge from a fixed reasoning structure. This reduces consistency across executions and fails to maintain the orderly, step-by-step reasoning required.

options.text: Build a Step Functions state machine where each reasoning phase of the ReAct pattern is represented as its own state. Assign a specific prompt to every stage and rely on its native retry and error-handling features to manage FM invocation failures.

correct_text: Build a Step Functions state machine where each reasoning phase of the ReAct pattern is represented as its own state. Assign a specific prompt to every stage and rely on its native retry and error-handling features to manage FM invocation failures.
concepto: Step Functions orquestando patron ReAct de FM

stem: An AI development team within a global fashion intelligence organization ingests extensive collections of videos and photos from international runway seasons, couture exhibitions, and street-style archives. The team applies a vision-oriented model to identify garment elements, fabric textures, and accessory groupings, along with a foundation-model workflow that interprets higher-level trend indicators detected in the visual data. Insights generated from this pipeline must support the creation of a fashion analytics dashboard used by research units to examine evolving patterns, evaluate regional differences, and forecast long-term style directions. Additionally, the platform also uses AWS App Runner for serving web-based analytics tools to users. Which of the following will satisfy this requirement with MINIMAL operational overhead?

options.text: Deploy Amazon EC2 instances with custom image-processing code. Store output in Amazon RDS and export data into an external analytics tool for dashboard generation.
options.rationale: because it typically requires manual infrastructure management (EC2 provisioning, scaling, patching) and adds complexity by using RDS plus an external analytics tool. This increases operational overhead compared to serverless alternatives.

options.text: Configure AWS Step Functions to coordinate processing tasks for all videos and photos by invoking Amazon Bedrock multimodal FMs. Store the structured outputs in Amazon S3, and publish fashion-trend metrics through an Amazon Quick Suite dashboard.

Train a fashion-classification model by using Amazon Rekognition Custom Labels. Store detection output in Amazon DynamoDB, and display trend metrics through Amazon Managed Grafana with custom plugins.
options.rationale: because Rekognition Custom Labels primarily requires training and dataset management, which adds operational effort. Additionally, Grafana with custom plugins introduces extra maintenance compared to Quick Suite’s native integration. This path is heavier than simply using Bedrock’s pre-trained multimodal models.

options.text: Route all videos and photos through an Amazon SageMaker AI Pipeline that calls a pre-trained model from the AWS Marketplace. Store inference results in Amazon S3 and present fashion metrics through Amazon Quick Suite.
options.rationale: because SageMaker pipelines involve more operational overhead (managing pipeline steps, monitoring, scaling). Even with Marketplace models, this approach is less lightweight than Bedrock, which removes the need for pipeline orchestration and infrastructure management.

correct_text: Configure AWS Step Functions to coordinate processing tasks for all videos and photos by invoking Amazon Bedrock multimodal FMs. Store the structured outputs in Amazon S3, and publish fashion-trend metrics through an Amazon Quick Suite dashboard.
concepto: Bedrock multimodal FMs + QuickSight dashboard GenAI

category: AIP – Implementation and Integration
stem: A company is developing a generative AI customer service application using Amazon Bedrock. The development team needs to frequently update the system prompts to refine the AI’s behavior and tone. The organization wants to decouple the prompt engineering lifecycle from the core application code deployment. Business analysts must be able to test different prompt variations, save specific versions, and transition these versions from a development environment to production seamlessly without requiring the engineering team to deploy new application code. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Store the system prompts in an Amazon S3 bucket. Configure an AWS Lambda function to retrieve the prompts during runtime. Update the text files in the S3 bucket when analysts need to change the prompt versions.
options.rationale: because, while storing prompts in Amazon S3 does decouple the text from the code, it simply lacks built-in version control, testing environments, and alias routing capabilities specifically designed for foundation models.

options.text: Use Bedrock Prompt Management to create, test, and version the prompts within the AWS Management Console. Configure the application to call the specific Bedrock API endpoint for the prompt version deployed to the production alias.

Hardcode the prompt strings within an AWS Step Functions state machine. Create a new version of the state machine each time the analysts require a prompt update, and update the Amazon API Gateway integration to point to the new state machine version.
options.rationale: because hardcoding strings into infrastructure updates still tightly couples the prompt engineering lifecycle to the deployment lifecycle, requiring operational overhead for every change.

options.text: Implement an Asynchronous processing model using Amazon SQS and AWS Lambda. Pass the new prompt versions as message payloads in the SQS queue, allowing the Lambda function to dynamically construct the prompt before invoking the foundation model.
options.rationale: because an asynchronous processing model via SQS is primarily designed for decoupling system components for scalability and resilience, not for versioning or managing the lifecycle of AI prompts.

correct_text: Use Bedrock Prompt Management to create, test, and version the prompts within the AWS Management Console. Configure the application to call the specific Bedrock API endpoint for the prompt version deployed to the production alias.
concepto: Bedrock Prompt Management versioning y alias

category: AIP – Operational Efficiency and Optimization for Generative AI Applications
stem: A global SaaS provider is designing a real-time virtual assistant powered by Amazon Bedrock using the Anthropic Claude 3 Haiku model. The assistant supports customer interactions across multiple continents and is expected to handle unpredictable traffic bursts. Under normal conditions, the system handles a consistent flow of requests, but during promotional campaigns and regional peak periods, request volume can surge to more than triple the usual rate. The application must consistently deliver responses within 2 seconds to maintain user experience SLAs (Service Level Agreements). Recent performance testing reveals that during sudden spikes, the model endpoints saturate, leading to throttling, increased latency, and intermittent request failures. The architecture must support seamless scaling across multiple AWS Regions while maximizing throughput efficiency and avoiding complex custom retry or routing mechanisms. Which solution provides the MOST effective way to handle these requirements?

options.text: Allocate a large number of provisioned throughput model units for Bedrock within a primary Region. Implement an application-layer retry strategy with exponential retry and circuit breaker patterns to manage throttled requests and transient failures.
options.rationale: because scaling provisioned throughput in a single region only creates a centralized scaling limit. Even with retry strategies such as exponential backoff and circuit breakers, this approach does not eliminate bottlenecks; it only delays failures. Additionally, retries increase response time, making it difficult to meet strict latency requirements.

options.text: Optimize inference efficiency by aggregating multiple prompts into batched requests and enable Cross-Region Inference in Bedrock using geography-aware inference profiles. Configure the application to invoke Region-specific endpoints that automatically distribute requests across available capacity within each geography.

Build a distributed application layer using AWS Lambda functions deployed in multiple regions. Implement a custom routing library that distributes requests using weighted round-robin logic and dynamically scales compute resources to handle increasing demand.
options.rationale: . While AWS Lambda can scale horizontally, this solution primarily focuses on application-layer scaling rather than model-layer scaling. The bottleneck occurs at the foundation model level, not the compute layer. Custom routing mechanisms also lack real-time awareness of model capacity, leading to inefficient traffic distribution.

options.text: Introduce an event-driven processing pipeline by buffering incoming requests in Amazon SQS queues and processing them asynchronously using worker services. Aggregate results and return responses to users once processing is complete.
options.rationale: because Amazon SQS introduces an asynchronous processing model, which is incompatible with the requirement for near real-time responses. This design adds latency and is better suited for background or batch processing workloads rather than interactive AI assistants.

correct_text: Optimize inference efficiency by aggregating multiple prompts into batched requests and enable Cross-Region Inference in Bedrock using geography-aware inference profiles. Configure the application to invoke Region-specific endpoints that automatically distribute requests across available capacity within each geography.
concepto: Cross-Region Inference profiles + batching Bedrock

category: AIP – Operational Efficiency and Optimization for Generative AI Applications
stem: A company is building a customer support AI-powered chatbot using Amazon Bedrock. The chatbot should be able to respond to simple product inquiries and more complex, reasoning-based questions. Simple product queries account for 75% of the total queries, while the more advanced queries make up 25%. The solution needs to be cost-effective, with minimal operational overhead, and must maintain high-quality responses. Additionally, the platform integrates Amazon Comprehend for sentiment analysis to further enhance the chatbot’s ability to understand customer intent and tone. Which approach would best address these requirements?

options.text: Deploy Bedrock with provisioned throughput, integrating the Anthropic Claude Sonnet model to process all query types. Utilize Amazon ElastiCache (Redis OSS) to store frequently accessed responses, setting a 24-hour TTL. Leverage Amazon CloudWatch to monitor cache efficiency and scale the provisioned capacity as traffic patterns change.
options.rationale: because this solution primarily uses Claude Sonnet for all queries, which is not cost-effective. Since 75% of the queries are simple product inquiries, using a more efficient model like Claude Haiku for those queries would be more cost-effective. Additionally, using Sonnet for all queries does not optimize resource usage based on query complexity.

options.text: Leverage Bedrock’s intelligent prompt routing to manage query distribution. Assign Anthropic Claude Haiku as the default model for handling simple inquiries and configure Claude Sonnet as the fallback for more complex queries. The routing mechanism will direct basic queries to Claude Haiku and route more intricate ones to Claude Sonnet.

Deploy a combination of Amazon Lex for handling simple product inquiries and Bedrock for complex reasoning tasks. Use Amazon S3 to store pre-generated answers to common queries and leverage Amazon CloudWatch to analyze query patterns and adjust model utilization accordingly.
options.rationale: . While Lex and Bedrock are useful, combining them typically introduces unnecessary complexity and operational overhead. Amazon Bedrock intelligent prompt routing is a simpler and more efficient solution for routing queries to the right model based on their complexity, without the need for managing multiple services like Lex and S3 for caching.

options.text: Integrate Amazon SageMaker AI to continuously fine-tune an existing Claude Sonnet model based on real-time user feedback and chat logs. Implement Amazon Kendra to retrieve contextual information from FAQs and product documentation, enhancing the accuracy of complex queries.
options.rationale: because this solution introduces significant operational overhead with continuous fine-tuning of the model and the integration of Amazon Kendra for context retrieval. While these may improve the accuracy of complex queries, they do not meet the requirement for a minimal operational overhead solution. Intelligent prompt routing provides an easier and more efficient way to manage query complexity without the need for constant model updates.

correct_text: Leverage Bedrock’s intelligent prompt routing to manage query distribution. Assign Anthropic Claude Haiku as the default model for handling simple inquiries and configure Claude Sonnet as the fallback for more complex queries. The routing mechanism will direct basic queries to Claude Haiku and route more intricate ones to Claude Sonnet.
concepto: Bedrock intelligent prompt routing (Haiku/Sonnet)

category: AIP – Testing, Validation, and Troubleshooting
stem: An enterprise is developing a RAG-based chatbot to provide answers from internal technical documentation, including PDF design documents, architecture diagrams, and policy manuals stored in Amazon S3. The company uses Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases for retrieval, with embeddings stored in S3 Vectors to help reduce retrieval costs. During ingestion, a fixed-chunking approach splits related sentences or clauses into separate chunks, causing some answers to lack context. Amazon SageMaker AI is also used to preprocess scanned documents using Amazon Textract endpoints, while a Bedrock foundation model generates responses from retrieved chunks. The enterprise seeks a configuration that ensures coherent retrieval, keeps answers relevant, and minimizes costs in this RAG document analysis workflow. Which configuration best meets the enterprise requirements?

options.text: Disable chunking and ingest entire documents as single chunks, then rely on the RetrieveAndGenerate API to handle long contexts.
options.rationale: because ingesting entire documents as single chunks dramatically increases token usage. Large chunks often exceed the model’s context window, forcing the system to truncate or ignore important information. While this approach might simply reduce the number of retrieval calls, it is not typically effective for ensuring coherent responses and often increases retrieval costs rather than reducing them. Foundation models generally perform best when provided with semantically coherent, manageable chunks rather than entire documents.

options.text: Deploy an Anthropic Claude model in Bedrock using the maximum context window, and apply recursive summarization to long documents before ingestion.
options.rationale: . Recursive summarization may reduce text length, but it can only approximate semantic boundaries and may omit critical details. This approach is typically more resource-intensive and increases preprocessing complexity, without guaranteeing that the retrieved chunks are contextually coherent for RAG workflows.

options.text: Activate semantic chunking in the Bedrock Knowledge Base. Optimize the maximum tokens parameter to base chunks on meaning.
Use hierarchical chunking to generate small child chunks and large parent chunks for retrieval.
options.rationale: . Hierarchical chunking is primarily helpful for multi-level document structures, but it can still produce child chunks that are semantically incomplete. Retrieving large parent chunks may include irrelevant content, which increases retrieval costs. This method simply shifts the problem from fragmented child chunks to oversized parent chunks, meaning it does not fully optimize token usage or relevance for foundation model responses.

correct_text: Activate semantic chunking in the Bedrock Knowledge Base. Optimize the maximum tokens parameter to base chunks on meaning.
concepto: Bedrock Knowledge Base semantic chunking

category: AIP – Foundation Model Integration, Data Management, and Compliance
stem: A development team is designing an AI-powered assistance platform that uses Amazon Bedrock to analyze customer inquiries and produce real-time replies. Several incoming messages contain personally identifiable information (PII), and the platform must comply with the company’s strict privacy rules. The solution must ensure that PII is masked before the model processes any input, that any sensitive information is removed from the model’s responses, and that stored interaction logs are kept only for the minimum retention window. The organization also requires that all log data follow approved PII storage and retention controls. To enhance downstream analytics, the team plans to incorporate Amazon SageMaker Clarify for detecting bias and monitoring the quality of processed data. Which approach satisfies these constraints?

options.text: Use Amazon Textract to extract text from stored interaction logs in Amazon S3 and analyze them for PII post-processing. Configure Amazon EventBridge to trigger Textract checks on new log files. Enforce retention timelines with S3 Lifecycle policies and monitor compliance using AWS Config.
options.rationale: because Amazon Textract analyzes data only after it has been stored in S3, which means raw PII is already collected and exposed before verification occurs. This does not meet the requirement to mask PII before inference, and the approach provides no protection during model processing. EventBridge and AWS Config help detect issues after storage, but do not prevent PII exposure at the model level.

options.text: Use Bedrock Guardrails to automatically mask PII in incoming requests before the model evaluates them and to redact sensitive data from model-generated responses. Save all interaction records in Amazon S3. Enable Amazon Macie to perform continuous inspection and alerting for sensitive information stored in S3. Apply S3 Lifecycle configurations to ensure logs are retained only for the mandated duration.

Use Amazon Rekognition text analysis to scan interaction logs stored in Amazon S3 for sensitive information. Store logs with server-side encryption using AWS KMS, configure IAM restrictions for access control, and apply S3 Lifecycle policies to transition stored logs to Glacier Deep Archive for long-term storage.
options.rationale: because Rekognition text detection is primarily designed for extracting text from images and cannot mask PII in real-time prompts sent to the model. The scanning still happens after data is written to S3, so unredacted PII can be processed by the model. Moving logs to Glacier Deep Archive also violates the requirement to retain data only for the minimum necessary period instead of archiving it long term.

options.text: Use Bedrock Guardrails to block and sanitize PII in both user inputs and model outputs. Store interaction data in Amazon S3 with AWS KMS–based encryption. Turn on AWS CloudTrail to capture Bedrock API activity and configure Amazon Macie to produce compliance findings for stored data. Set S3 Lifecycle rules to govern how long log files remain in storage.
options.rationale: . Although Guardrails provides PII filtering, this option focuses on encryption, logging, and compliance reporting, which do not guarantee that sensitive data is removed within the required retention window. CloudTrail and Macie do not delete or prevent unnecessary storage of PII, and the setup may still allow sensitive information to persist longer than allowed.

correct_text: Use Bedrock Guardrails to automatically mask PII in incoming requests before the model evaluates them and to redact sensitive data from model-generated responses. Save all interaction records in Amazon S3. Enable Amazon Macie to perform continuous inspection and alerting for sensitive information stored in S3. Apply S3 Lifecycle configurations to ensure logs are retained only for the mandated duration.
concepto: Bedrock Guardrails PII masking + Macie/S3 lifecycle

category: AIP – Foundation Model Integration, Data Management, and Compliance
stem: A global SaaS company is deploying a customer‑support Amazon Bedrock–based chatbot to assist users in Europe, Asia, and North America. The chatbot uses Amazon SageMaker AI to run a risk‑scoring model on customer account data, and Amazon Comprehend to classify the support request’s sentiment and detect urgency. Recently, customers in one AWS Region have begun seeing error messages indicating API throttling and higher latency when calling the Amazon Bedrock API, particularly during peak hours. To improve resilience and reliability, the architecture team wants a deployment strategy that prevents a single Region from becoming a bottleneck or single point of failure while maintaining compliance within each geographic area. The solution must also ensure that failover remains transparent to the application without requiring manual routing logic in the client. Which solution will best address these requirements?

options.text: Use Amazon Route 53 latency-based routing to distribute client traffic across multiple Bedrock API endpoints deployed in different Regions.
options.rationale: . Latency-based routing can help direct requests to the nearest Region, but it typically does not account for real-time load or capacity limits on the Bedrock endpoints. As a result, some requests may still hit throttled or overutilized Regions, generating error messages. While latency routing improves performance under normal conditions, it simply does not provide the automated failover and load-sharing capabilities offered by cross-Region inference.

options.text: Utilized Amazon Route 53 weighted routing to direct traffic to one primary Region and fail over to a secondary Region only if the primary endpoint fails.
options.rationale: . Weighted routing with manual failover is primarily reactive rather than proactive. It only shifts traffic when a Region is detected as unavailable, which means requests can still experience throttling or high latency in the primary Region before failover occurs. This approach does not automatically distribute load across multiple Regions simultaneously, making it simply less effective than cross-region inference for handling peak traffic.

options.text: Deploy all Bedrock API calls to a single Region and scale up the endpoint to handle peak traffic. Rely on Amazon CloudWatch alarms to trigger scaling.
options.rationale: . Using a single Region creates a single point of failure and relies on reactive scaling. CloudWatch alarms may take time to trigger, during which users could continue experiencing error messages or high latency. This method addresses throughput only after the fact and does not proactively balance traffic across multiple Regions, making it typically unsuitable for globally distributed applications that require high availability.

options.text: Enable cross-region inference to automatically distribute Bedrock API traffic across multiple AWS Regions within the same geographic area.

correct_text: Enable cross-region inference to automatically distribute Bedrock API traffic across multiple AWS Regions within the same geographic area.
concepto: Bedrock cross-region inference para resiliencia

category: AIP – AI Safety, Security, and Governance
stem: A global telecommunications provider is building a generative AI (GenAI) application using Amazon Bedrock to detect usage anomalies and predict subscriber churn across its international customer base. The application ingests and processes billions of subscriber activity records daily across AWS Regions in Europe, North America, and Asia, then stores all outputs in Amazon S3. Regional telecommunications regulations mandate that subscriber data must be processed and stored exclusively within the AWS Region where it originates. The application must also maintain a tamper-proof audit trail of all AI-generated outputs and automatically discover and classify personally identifiable subscriber data at rest within each Region-specific S3 bucket. Which approach satisfies all of these requirements?

options.text: Use Bedrock cross-Region inference profiles to restrict model invocations to each subscriber's Region of origin. Apply IAM permission boundaries to all regional service roles to enforce access controls. Use Amazon CloudWatch Logs to record all AI recommendation outputs. Use Amazon Comprehend to scan and classify personally identifiable subscriber data in each Region.
options.rationale: because Amazon Bedrock cross-Region inference profiles control where model inference is executed but do not enforce data residency at the storage layer, subscriber records in Amazon S3 remain unprotected from cross-Region movement without S3 Object Lock and Region-specific bucket policies. IAM permission boundaries define the maximum permissions available to an IAM entity but cannot physically prevent data from being transferred to another Region. Amazon CloudWatch Logs are not immutable; log streams can be deleted within the configured retention window, which does not satisfy the tamper-proof audit requirement. Amazon Comprehend is a natural language processing service designed to extract entities and sentiment from unstructured text—it is not designed for discovering and classifying sensitive data stored in S3, which is the purpose-built function of Amazon Macie.

options.text: Use AWS Organizations SCPs to restrict data ingestion and storage operations to the subscriber's Region of origin. Import a custom foundation model into Bedrock and deploy it to each regional jurisdiction. Use AWS CloudTrail immutable logs to audit all AI-generated outputs and model invocations.
options.rationale: because Service Control Policies set permission guardrails at the AWS account level and can restrict which API actions are available in which Regions, but they simply do not enforce data residency at the object level within Amazon S3, subscriber data can still exist in or be copied to buckets outside the approved Region without additional storage-layer controls such as S3 Object Lock and Region-specific bucket policies. Importing and deploying a custom foundation model to each regional jurisdiction addresses where inference runs but does not control where processed outputs are stored at rest. This option also omits Amazon Macie entirely, leaving the automated data discovery and classification requirement unaddressed.

options.text: Use S3 Object Lock with Region-specific S3 bucket policies to enforce data residency for all subscriber records. Pre-process all subscriber activity records within the originating AWS Region before sending them to Bedrock. Use Amazon Macie to discover and classify personally identifiable subscriber data. Use AWS CloudTrail immutable logs to audit all AI-generated outputs.

Use AWS Glue crawlers per Region to catalog and tag personally identifiable subscriber data across all regional S3 buckets. Use Amazon Athena with Region-scoped workgroups to restrict query execution to the originating AWS Region. Use AWS Config rules to detect and remediate cross-Region S3 data transfers. Use Amazon CloudWatch Logs to capture and retain all AI-generated outputs for audit compliance.
options.rationale: because AWS Glue crawlers scan and catalog data in S3 by building metadata entries in the AWS Glue Data Catalog, but cataloging does not enforce data residency, it does not prevent subscriber records from being accessed or copied across Regions, and it does not replace the object-level immutability and boundary enforcement that Amazon S3 Object Lock and Region-specific bucket policies provide. Amazon Athena Region-scoped workgroups control where SQL queries are executed but have no effect on where the underlying S3 data is physically stored or whether it can move across Regions. AWS Config rules primarily detect configuration drift and non-compliant resource states but do not produce tamper-proof, non-repudiable audit logs. Amazon CloudWatch Logs are also not immutable; log streams can be deleted within the configured retention window, which does not satisfy the tamper-proof audit trail requirement.

correct_text: Use S3 Object Lock with Region-specific S3 bucket policies to enforce data residency for all subscriber records. Pre-process all subscriber activity records within the originating AWS Region before sending them to Bedrock. Use Amazon Macie to discover and classify personally identifiable subscriber data. Use AWS CloudTrail immutable logs to audit all AI-generated outputs.
concepto: S3 Object Lock residencia + Macie + CloudTrail GenAI outputs

category: AIP – AI Safety, Security, and Governance
stem: A healthcare technology organization is developing a generative AI assistant to analyze medical procedure reports involving its devices. These reports are securely transferred from on-premises clinical record systems to an Amazon S3 bucket using AWS DataSync immediately after publication and are indexed using an Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases configuration. The application adheres to strict privacy policies. Surgeons must be able to view patient information, while engineers must receive responses where patient information is masked using PII detection controls. The assistant authenticates users with Amazon Cognito. The AI assistant must reference only medical reports published within the last three years. Which solution satisfies these requirements?

options.text: Enable Amazon Macie PII detection on the S3 bucket and configure an S3 event trigger to invoke AWS Lambda that redacts sensitive information before storing the document. Configure the Lambda function to remove outdated reports and re-sync the knowledge base.
options.rationale: because enabling Amazon Macie and permanently redacting PII during ingestion only removes sensitive information from the original documents before they are stored. This violates the requirement that surgeons must still be able to view patient information. Once PII is removed at ingestion time, the information cannot be recovered for authorized users, making the solution incompatible with role-based visibility requirements.

options.text: Trigger an AWS Lambda function when new reports are uploaded to synchronize the S3 bucket with the Bedrock Knowledge Base. Use another Lambda function with Amazon Comprehend PII detection to redact sensitive information for engineers. Configure S3 Lifecycle rules to delete reports older than three years.
options.rationale: because performing PII detection and redaction using Amazon Comprehend during ingestion just results in inconsistent data visibility across users and couples privacy enforcement with the ingestion pipeline. Engineers and surgeons would end up referencing different versions of documents or partially modified data. Additionally, this approach introduces unnecessary operational complexity and does not leverage Bedrock guardrails designed specifically for response-level filtering in generative AI systems.

options.text: Configure an S3 Lifecycle policy to automatically remove reports older than three years. Schedule an AWS Lambda function to periodically synchronize the bucket contents with the knowledge base. When users interact with the AI assistant, it uses PII detection and applies Bedrock guardrails dynamically, based on the authenticated user’s Cognito user group, to redact PII from responses when required.

Create a second Bedrock Knowledge Base containing reports where PII has been redacted using AWS Lambda and Amazon Comprehend PII detection. Route engineers to the sanitized knowledge base and surgeons to the original knowledge base based on Cognito group membership.
options.rationale: because maintaining two separate knowledge bases simply creates unnecessary duplication of data and introduces the risk of synchronization drift between sanitized and original datasets. This approach increases operational overhead and storage costs while complicating data management. A role-based guardrail applied at inference time achieves the same privacy requirements more efficiently while maintaining a single authoritative source of medical reports.

correct_text: Configure an S3 Lifecycle policy to automatically remove reports older than three years. Schedule an AWS Lambda function to periodically synchronize the bucket contents with the knowledge base. When users interact with the AI assistant, it uses PII detection and applies Bedrock guardrails dynamically, based on the authenticated user’s Cognito user group, to redact PII from responses when required.
concepto: Guardrails dinamicos por grupo Cognito + KB sync

category: AIP – AI Safety, Security, and Governance
stem: An organization is developing an AI-driven system for content moderation and product description generation. The system produces refined product descriptions, safety disclaimers, and localization-ready translations for millions of seller-submitted listings. To ensure outputs comply with marketplace policies across regions and product categories, the compliance team must evaluate multiple foundation models. The organization integrates Amazon Rekognition to analyze product images for unsafe or restricted items and Amazon Translate to generate multilingual reference descriptions for testing cross-language consistency. The team has also considered reranker models to compare output consistency across foundation models. The solution requires an automated, scalable method to assess model outputs for correctness, policy alignment, harmful content detection, and multilingual fidelity, as manual review and keyword-based filtering are insufficient. Which solution best satisfies the compliance and evaluation requirements?

options.text: Run RAG evaluation for Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases to assess retrieval accuracy and completeness of content across product categories.
options.rationale: . Running the RAG evaluation for Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases primarily measures retrieval accuracy and document coverage across categories. It does not evaluate reasoning quality, policy compliance, or the detection of harmful content. This method simply assesses whether relevant content is present, making it insufficient for systematic model evaluation.

options.text: Use AWS Lambda functions with keyword lists and regex to flag potential policy violations, calculate violation counts per model, and evaluate basic text properties like length and repetition.
options.rationale: . Using AWS Lambda with keyword lists and regex can only flag obvious policy violations and compute basic text metrics such as length or repetition. It typically cannot understand context, detect nuanced harmful content, or evaluate multilingual fidelity. This approach simply lacks the sophistication needed to score reasoning quality or policy alignment.

options.text: Implement Amazon OpenSearch for full-text indexing of generated descriptions and manually compare vector similarity scores to determine which model performs better.
options.rationale: . Implementing Amazon OpenSearch for full-text indexing and comparing vector similarity scores only measures textual similarity, not correctness or compliance. It primarily captures surface-level matches and does not assess reasoning, harmful content, or alignment with organizational policies.

options.text: Use LLM-as-a-judge within Amazon Bedrock Model Evaluation to automatically score generated product descriptions for policy compliance, contextual safety, multilingual accuracy, and consistency.

correct_text: Use LLM-as-a-judge within Amazon Bedrock Model Evaluation to automatically score generated product descriptions for policy compliance, contextual safety, multilingual accuracy, and consistency.
concepto: LLM-as-a-judge en Bedrock Model Evaluation

category: AIP – Implementation and Integration
stem: A company is developing a generative AI (GenAI) application that converts large-scale academic content into structured learning materials. The application ingests heterogeneous data formats, including PDFs, presentation slides, word processing documents, and recorded video sessions. The system processes more than 10,000 content items per day with bursts of up to 500 concurrent uploads. The solution must interpret both textual and audio-based inputs, extract main points, and generate accurate summaries. The application uses prompt flows to standardize summarization logic across different content types. The processed outputs must support version tracking. The application must also enable multiple users to collaborate on the generated materials in real time. Which solution satisfies these requirements?

options.text: Use Amazon Bedrock Data Automation with AWS Lambda to coordinate ingestion and manage prompt flows. Use Bedrock Knowledge Bases to process both document and multimedia content. Store generated outputs in Amazon DynamoDB with version attributes. Enable collaboration using Amazon SNS and Amazon SQS for event-driven updates.
options.rationale: because Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases is primarily used for retrieval over indexed data and not for processing multimedia inputs. Amazon DynamoDB simply stores key-value data and is not suitable for managing large versioned content outputs. Additionally, Amazon SNS and Amazon SQS only provide event-driven messaging and do not support real-time collaborative interactions.

options.text: Use Amazon Bedrock Data Automation (BDA) with foundation models (FMs) to process content and generate summaries across diverse inputs. Leverage Amazon Transcribe to convert audio from multimedia inputs into text and Amazon Textract to derive structured data from document-based sources. Store generated artifacts in Amazon S3 with versioning enabled, and maintain associated metadata in Amazon DynamoDB. Enable synchronized multi-user interactions and real-time updates using AWS AppSync GraphQL subscriptions.

Use Amazon Bedrock Data Automation with AWS Step Functions to orchestrate prompt flows and processing pipelines. Use Amazon Textract and Amazon Transcribe for content extraction. Store processed outputs in Amazon Aurora with version columns. Enable real-time collaboration using Amazon API Gateway WebSocket APIs backed by AWS Lambda.
options.rationale: because Amazon Aurora is designed for relational workloads and is not optimized for storing large unstructured content with version tracking. While WebSocket APIs can enable communication, they simply require custom state management and do not provide the managed real-time synchronization capabilities of AWS AppSync.

options.text: Use Amazon Bedrock Data Automation with Amazon Textract and Amazon Transcribe to process all content types. Store outputs in Amazon S3 with versioning enabled. Manage prompt flows using Amazon EventBridge and coordinate collaboration using Amazon CloudFront with Amazon API Gateway.
