options.rationale: because Amazon EventBridge is used for event routing and does not manage prompt flow logic. Amazon CloudFront simply delivers content and does not support real-time collaborative data updates, even when combined with API Gateway.

correct_text: Use Amazon Bedrock Data Automation (BDA) with foundation models (FMs) to process content and generate summaries across diverse inputs. Leverage Amazon Transcribe to convert audio from multimedia inputs into text and Amazon Textract to derive structured data from document-based sources. Store generated artifacts in Amazon S3 with versioning enabled, and maintain associated metadata in Amazon DynamoDB. Enable synchronized multi-user interactions and real-time updates using AWS AppSync GraphQL subscriptions.
concepto: Bedrock Data Automation (BDA) multimodal

category: AIP – AI Safety, Security, and Governance
stem: A financial technology enterprise is modernizing its analytics and customer-engagement platforms. As part of this transformation, the organization is integrating Amazon Bedrock with Amazon SageMaker pipelines to support a new conversational AI system capable of processing regulated financial data. The AI system will respond to customer inquiries, summarize account-related insights, and provide guidance about financial products. The security team requires strict prevention of harmful output, elimination of unauthorized sensitive data disclosures, and automated detection and blocking of any content that may indicate illegal activity. Which of the following will satisfy the given requirements with MINIMAL effort?

options.text: Use Amazon Macie to inspect model responses for sensitive data. Integrate Amazon SNS notifications to trigger alerts when potentially illegal content is detected. Apply basic prompt constraints in Bedrock to limit harmful output.
options.rationale: because Amazon Macie is primarily designed for data classification and discovery in S3, not for real-time inspection of conversational AI responses. This approach requires custom integrations and manual effort, which does not meet the requirement of minimal effort.

options.text: Configure generic safe completion settings in Bedrock Guardrails to intercept harmful or restricted content. Add AWS WAF rules to block prohibited content. Set up an Amazon CloudWatch alarm that triggers an AWS Lambda function to review and suppress responses that may contain sensitive information.
options.rationale: because while it uses Bedrock Guardrails, it adds unnecessary complexity with WAF, CloudWatch, and Lambda. This multi-service setup increases operational overhead and is not the most efficient or minimal-effort solution.

options.text: Use SageMaker Clarify reports to identify unsafe conversation patterns. Rely on prompt-level boundaries within Bedrock to limit sensitive data responses. Set up an Amazon CloudWatch metric filters to capture interactions that may contain illegal content indicators.
options.rationale: because SageMaker Clarify is typically used for bias detection and explainability in ML models, not real-time harmful content filtering. CloudWatch metric filters are reactive rather than proactive, meaning unsafe outputs could still reach customers before being flagged.

options.text: Configure content filters using Bedrock Guardrails to intercept harmful or restricted content. Add word filters within Bedrock Guardrails to block prohibited or illegal content. Enable contextual grounding checks in Bedrock to ensure responses do not reveal sensitive information.

correct_text: Configure content filters using Bedrock Guardrails to intercept harmful or restricted content. Add word filters within Bedrock Guardrails to block prohibited or illegal content. Enable contextual grounding checks in Bedrock to ensure responses do not reveal sensitive information.
concepto: Bedrock Guardrails content/word filters + grounding

category: AIP – Operational Efficiency and Optimization for Generative AI Applications
stem: A fintech company is developing a customer support chatbot that must provide accurate, context-aware responses by retrieving information from its extensive knowledge base of financial product documentation, regulatory guidelines, and customer FAQs. The solution uses Amazon Bedrock with Anthropic Claude Sonnet for response generation and requires real-time inference with sub-second latency to maintain user engagement. The development team has implemented a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) architecture using a vector store to search through 50,000+ document chunks, but the solution is experiencing inference latency issues averaging 3-4 seconds per query, which exceeds the 1-second SLA. The team needs to optimize the solution while maintaining response accuracy and ensuring the system can scale to handle 10,000 concurrent users during peak hours. What should the development team implement to meet the sub-second latency SLA while maintaining response accuracy and supporting peak load?

options.text: Switch to Anthropic Claude Haiku for faster inference performance, implement hybrid search with metadata filtering to reduce the candidate set before vector similarity search, and use an inference profile with cross-region routing to distribute load across multiple AWS regions for improved availability and reduced latency during peak hours.

Increase the number of model units (MU) provisioned for Claude Sonnet to improve throughput, implement exponential retry logic to handle transient failures, and enable Container Insights in Amazon CloudWatch to monitor the vector store query performance without changing the retrieval or chunking strategy.
options.rationale: because increasing model units only improves concurrent request capacity and throughput, not the per-request inference latency. Claude Sonnet will still require 3-4 seconds per inference regardless of how many MUs are provisioned, failing to meet the sub-second SLA requirement. Additionally, exponential retry logic addresses transient failures but actually increases latency rather than reducing it, and monitoring alone without addressing the root cause (model inference speed) cannot solve the performance problem.

options.text: Replace the vector store with Amazon Kendra for semantic search, implement batch inference instead of real-time inference to reduce costs, and use the default chunking provided by Bedrock Knowledge Bases to simplify the implementation and improve response times.
options.rationale: because batch inference processes requests in queued batches with processing delays ranging from minutes to hours, making it completely unsuitable for real-time customer support that requires sub-second response times and immediate user engagement. While Amazon Kendra primarily provides excellent semantic search capabilities, switching to batch inference fundamentally contradicts the real-time inference requirement stated in the scenario and would severely degrade the user experience.

options.text: Implement prompt caching to cache frequently retrieved document chunks for common financial product inquiries and reuse them across similar queries, switch to Bedrock Provisioned Throughput with Claude Opus for guaranteed capacity and improved response quality, and optimize the retrieval strategy to fetch only the top 3 most relevant chunks instead of 10 to reduce context size.
options.rationale: because Claude Opus is the largest and most capable model in the Claude family but also has the highest inference latency (typically 5-8 seconds for complex prompts), making it move in the opposite direction from the sub-second requirement—it would actually worsen the latency problem rather than solve it. While prompt caching and reducing the number of retrieved chunks may provide marginal improvements, these optimizations cannot overcome Claude Opus’s inherently slower inference speed, which is fundamentally incompatible with the sub-second SLA.

correct_text: Switch to Anthropic Claude Haiku for faster inference performance, implement hybrid search with metadata filtering to reduce the candidate set before vector similarity search, and use an inference profile with cross-region routing to distribute load across multiple AWS regions for improved availability and reduced latency during peak hours.
concepto: Haiku + hybrid search + inference profile cross-region

category: AIP – Operational Efficiency and Optimization for Generative AI Applications
stem: A law firm operates an internal Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) assistant built on Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases, enabling staff to search through regulatory documents and compliance guidance stored in the firm’s knowledge repository. The repository contains tens of thousands of documents that are continuously updated as new guidance is issued. The assistant streams answers through the RetrieveAndGenerateStream API. The assistant is producing suboptimal responses and occasional hallucinations because the initial retrieval step relies solely on semantic similarity, surfacing documents that appear contextually close to the query but are not actually relevant to the question. The firm wants to improve retrieval accuracy with the least possible additional infrastructure. Which approach achieves this outcome with the minimum operational overhead?

options.text: Deploy a custom cross-encoder reranking model on a dedicated Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint, fronted by an Application Load Balancer. Configure the assistant to invoke this endpoint for every query, rescoring candidate documents prior to generating a response
options.rationale: because Amazon SageMaker AI is primarily a fully managed machine learning platform used to build, train, and host custom models, including cross-encoder rerankers, on dedicated inference endpoints. While this approach is technically capable of improving retrieval relevance, it requires the firm to build and maintain its own reranking model, manage endpoint scaling and availability, and operate an Application Load Balancer — all of which add significant infrastructure overhead. Amazon Bedrock already provides fully managed reranker models that can be activated through a simple configuration change inside Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases, making a custom SageMaker-hosted solution far more complex than necessary.

options.text: Deploy an Amazon Neptune graph database to model relationships between documents, and use computed centrality scores to rank retrieved results prior to generating responses.
options.rationale: because Amazon Neptune is a purpose-built managed graph database designed to store and query highly connected datasets using graph query languages such as Gremlin and openCypher. While computing centrality scores across a document relationship graph is a valid relevance technique in other contexts, applying it here means provisioning a Neptune cluster, modeling and maintaining the firm’s entire document graph, and keeping it continuously synchronized with the knowledge base. This just introduces significant infrastructure and operational costs that are entirely unnecessary.

options.text: Use Bedrock Knowledge Bases Retrieve API to pull an initial set of candidate documents, invoke the Bedrock Rerank API as a standalone call to reorder those documents by relevance, and then call InvokeModelWithResponseStream to generate and stream the response to the user.
options.rationale: because although the Amazon Bedrock Rerank API is a valid managed service that reorders retrieved documents against a query using a dedicated reranker model, wiring it together with the Retrieve API and InvokeModelWithResponseStream as three independent calls means the firm must own the full orchestration logic: passing outputs between each step, handling errors across calls, and maintaining that custom code over time. This approach would improve relevance and reduce hallucinations, but it solves the problem the hard way. Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases already expose reranking as a built-in configuration option that operates transparently within the existing RetrieveAndGenerateStream API call, making a manually assembled multi-step pipeline unnecessary.

options.text: Configure the built-in reranking capability of Bedrock Knowledge Bases with the latest available Bedrock reranker models, allowing retrieved documents to be automatically rescored based on contextual relevance prior to response generation.

correct_text: Configure the built-in reranking capability of Bedrock Knowledge Bases with the latest available Bedrock reranker models, allowing retrieved documents to be automatically rescored based on contextual relevance prior to response generation.
concepto: Bedrock Knowledge Base built-in reranking

category: AIP – Foundation Model Integration, Data Management, and Compliance
stem: An e-commerce company uses Amazon Bedrock to power an AI assistant that answers product, shipping, and return questions. Usage analysis shows that many customers submit semantically equivalent questions using different wording, causing the application to make repeated requests to the foundation model for answers that have already been generated. The company wants to reduce redundant model calls, return consistent answers for similar questions, and maintain low latency during periods of heavy customer traffic. The solution should reuse previously generated query-response pairs whenever a new query is sufficiently similar to an earlier request. Which approach will satisfy these requirements?

options.text: Store previously answered questions and responses in Amazon DynamoDB. Normalize each incoming query and use the normalized text as the partition key to return an existing response when an exact match is found.
options.rationale: because this approach would typically match only queries that normalize to the same key. Customers can express the same intent with substantially different words, so exact-key lookups do not inherently identify semantic similarity between differently phrased questions.

options.text: Cache completed Bedrock responses in Amazon ElastiCache by using a hash of each customer query as the cache key. Return the cached response when the same query is submitted again, and invoke Bedrock for cache misses.
options.rationale: because a hash-based cache primarily detects identical input values. Even small wording changes can produce a different cache key, causing the application to invoke Amazon Bedrock again despite an equivalent response already existing.

options.text: Index the query-response pairs in Amazon OpenSearch Service and use standard keyword-based search to locate previously answered questions. Return the response from the highest-scoring document when the keyword relevance score exceeds a configured threshold.
options.rationale: because keyword search would simply emphasize lexical overlap between queries. Amazon OpenSearch vector search instead compares embeddings that represent semantic meaning, making it better suited to finding equivalent questions that use different terminology or sentence structures.

options.text: Use Amazon OpenSearch Service as a semantic cache by storing embeddings for previously answered query-response pairs in a k-nearest neighbor (k-NN) index. For each new query, generate its embedding and perform an approximate k-NN search to identify a sufficiently similar previous query. Return the associated cached response when a suitable match is found instead of making another Bedrock model call.

correct_text: Use Amazon OpenSearch Service as a semantic cache by storing embeddings for previously answered query-response pairs in a k-nearest neighbor (k-NN) index. For each new query, generate its embedding and perform an approximate k-NN search to identify a sufficiently similar previous query. Return the associated cached response when a suitable match is found instead of making another Bedrock model call.
concepto: Semantic cache con OpenSearch k-NN para FM

category: AIP – Implementation and Integration
stem: A development team is tasked with enhancing the troubleshooting capabilities of the foundation model (FM) application. The application is designed to manage customer interactions in real-time, incorporating both AI-driven natural language processing (NLP) for analyzing customer inquiries and machine vision for detecting product issues. The team needs to address issues related to analyzing error patterns in the system, tracing API calls, and improving troubleshooting efficiency. The solution should enable the team to analyze logs from multiple sources, trace API calls across different services, and detect GenAI-specific error patterns automatically. The ideal solution should also support the application’s evolving AI models and enhance response time to identified issues.

options.text: Which of the following solutions will

Deploy Amazon CloudWatch Logs Insights to aggregate and analyze logs from the FM application, use Amazon SageMaker AI to perform machine learning-based anomaly detection on logs, and integrate AWS Lambda to trigger real-time alerts and responses based on detected errors in the logs.
options.rationale: because it lacks native support for GenAI error detection and distributed tracing. SageMaker anomaly detection typically requires custom model development and doesn’t offer built-in observability for GenAI workloads.

options.text: Set up Amazon CloudWatch Logs Insights for querying and correlating real-time application logs, utilize AWS X-Ray to trace API calls between the FM application and external data sources, and integrate Amazon Q Developer for GenAI-driven error pattern recognition to highlight error trends in the system.

Use Amazon CloudWatch Logs Insights to perform detailed log analysis for different error types, configure AWS X-Ray to trace API calls between internal microservices, and incorporate AWS Glue to automate the extraction and transformation of error data for further analysis.
options.rationale: because AWS Glue is primarily designed for batch ETL workflows, not real-time troubleshooting. It introduces latency and complexity without addressing GenAI-specific error visibility or enhancing response time.

options.text: Implement Amazon CloudWatch Logs Insights to gather logs from the application’s interactions with external APIs, use AWS X-Ray to monitor and trace the service calls that interface with GenAI models, and deploy Amazon Kinesis to stream and analyze real-time error data for further troubleshooting insights.
options.rationale: because while Kinesis supports real-time streaming, it doesn’t provide built-in GenAI observability or automated error pattern recognition. This setup lacks the targeted capabilities needed to support evolving GenAI models and efficient troubleshooting.

correct_text: Set up Amazon CloudWatch Logs Insights for querying and correlating real-time application logs, utilize AWS X-Ray to trace API calls between the FM application and external data sources, and integrate Amazon Q Developer for GenAI-driven error pattern recognition to highlight error trends in the system.
concepto: CloudWatch Logs Insights + X-Ray + Q Developer GenAI

category: AIP – Testing, Validation, and Troubleshooting
stem: A company is developing a generative AI assistant that delivers personalized product recommendations, promotional messages, and customer support summaries. The assistant leverages structured purchase history, behavioral data, and unstructured customer reviews to generate customized content in real time. To ensure outputs are accurate, relevant, and unbiased, the team plans to conduct systematic model evaluation across multiple AI model versions before deploying to the full customer base. The solution integrates Amazon Comprehend to extract sentiment, entities, and key themes from reviews and messages, and Amazon SageMaker AI to train predictive models that score engagement likelihood and product interest. The team requires a deployment strategy that enables safe testing of multiple AI model versions while collecting performance and evaluation metrics to inform decision-making. Which deployment strategy is most appropriate for this scenario?

options.text: Deploy the new AI model using a Blue/Green strategy, running it in parallel with the current model, and switch all traffic after verifying stability and metrics from Comprehend and SageMaker AI.
options.rationale: . Blue/Green deployment is primarily designed to ensure a smooth switch between model versions with minimal downtime. While it provides operational safety, it simply does not allow simultaneous comparison of multiple AI model versions. It evaluates only a single model in production at a time, limiting systematic evaluation and preventing direct comparisons of metrics such as sentiment, entity recognition, and predicted engagement.

options.text: Deploy the new AI model as a Canary Release to a small subset of users, monitor sentiment, entity extraction, and engagement scores with Comprehend and SageMaker AI, and gradually increase traffic if results meet quality standards.
options.rationale: . Canary deployment is typically used to release a new model to a small subset of users first, gradually increasing traffic while monitoring metrics. Although it helps detect early issues and reduce risk, it only evaluates one model version at a time, making it unsuitable for systematic comparison across multiple AI models. It does not support real-time evaluation of competing models for data-driven decision-making.

options.text: Utilize an A/B testing strategy to route different user segments to multiple AI model versions simultaneously, collect metrics such as sentiment, entity recognition, and predicted engagement using Comprehend and SageMaker AI, and select the best-performing model based on the comparison.
Implement a Linear deployment. Gradually shift user traffic to the new AI model in fixed increments and monitor the performance and engagement metrics.
options.rationale: . Linear deployment gradually shifts user traffic to the new model in fixed increments. This approach focuses solely on a safe, incremental rollout, providing controlled exposure to the latest model. However, it does not support parallel evaluation of multiple versions, which is essential for systematic model evaluation. Linear deployment is primarily about risk mitigation rather than model comparison or optimization.

correct_text: Utilize an A/B testing strategy to route different user segments to multiple AI model versions simultaneously, collect metrics such as sentiment, entity recognition, and predicted engagement using Comprehend and SageMaker AI, and select the best-performing model based on the comparison.
concepto: A/B testing de versiones de modelo GenAI

category: AIP – Operational Efficiency and Optimization for Generative AI Applications
stem: A company is developing a generative AI (GenAI) application to resolve complex healthcare questions. To prevent semantic dilution and minimize ambiguity, the application must cross-reference highly technical medical terminology against a private database of clinical documents. Furthermore, the underlying infrastructure must sustain a throughput of 1,000 queries per minute while maintaining a strict response latency of under 2 seconds. Which solution satisfies these demands with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Store the reference medical documents in an Amazon Kendra index. Deploy an Amazon Bedrock agent configured to use AWS Step Functions to manually process query decomposition before retrieving data, ensuring the application mitigates semantic dilution.
options.rationale: because building a custom orchestration pipeline with AWS Step Functions and an Amazon Bedrock agent primarily introduces significant operational overhead and latency, making it extremely difficult to meet the strict sub-2-second response time requirement.

options.text: Set up an knowledge base to house the reference medical documents, enabling native query decomposition to reduce semantic dilution. Build an Amazon Bedrock flow that directly links a foundation model (FM) to the knowledge base, delivering efficient access for the application.

Deploy custom machine learning (ML) models for query decomposition and terminology expansion using Amazon SageMaker AI. Securely store and index the reference medical documents in an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base.
options.rationale: because building, training, and hosting custom machine learning models on Amazon SageMaker specifically for query decomposition introduces immense operational overhead and infrastructure costs. Native Bedrock capabilities should be used instead to minimize this operational burden.

options.text: Ingest the medical documents into an Amazon OpenSearch Serverless vector collection. Configure an Amazon Bedrock agent equipped with advanced prompt templates to execute query decomposition. Route the finalized prompt through an Amazon API Gateway to generate the response.
options.rationale: because manually configuring an Amazon Bedrock agent to perform query decomposition via prompt engineering just increases operational complexity and latency. Agents are better suited for action execution (tool calling) rather than serving as a low-latency, high-throughput RAG retrieval proxy.

correct_text: Set up an knowledge base to house the reference medical documents, enabling native query decomposition to reduce semantic dilution. Build an Amazon Bedrock flow that directly links a foundation model (FM) to the knowledge base, delivering efficient access for the application.
concepto: Knowledge Base query decomposition + Bedrock flow

category: AIP – Foundation Model Integration, Data Management, and Compliance
stem: An AI development team is building a large-scale customer feedback summarization system using Amazon Bedrock and Amazon SageMaker AI. The system processes prompts from various sources, including social media posts, surveys, and online reviews. These prompts, along with the corresponding generated summaries, are stored in Amazon S3 for analysis and auditing purposes. Due to new regulatory requirements, the team needs to implement a robust governance framework that ensures all interactions with Bedrock are logged for compliance and that the lineage of each prompt and summary is traceable. Additionally, the team must be able to track the template versions and model invocations used to generate the summaries. Which of the following will satisfy the given requirements?

options.text: Leverage Amazon Data Firehose to stream prompt data into S3 for real-time storage. Use AWS Lambda functions to parse and store model invocation logs in Amazon DynamoDB, and enable Amazon CloudWatch to monitor all interactions with prompts and summaries.
options.rationale: because it only focuses on streaming and monitoring but does not provide native compliance logging of Amazon Bedrock API calls or prompt lineage, leaving regulatory requirements unmet.

options.text: Set up an Amazon Kinesis Data Stream to capture real-time prompt and summary data, and use Amazon Athena for querying and auditing the metadata stored in S3.
options.rationale: because while it enables streaming and querying, it does not address the need for governance of Bedrock interactions or tracking of template versions and model invocation metadata.

options.text: Save prompts and summaries in Amazon DynamoDB with additional metadata attributes, and utilize DynamoDB Streams to trigger AWS Lambda functions for processing updates related to lineage and metadata tracking.
options.rationale: because although DynamoDB primarily store metadata and Streams can process lineage updates, it lacks compliance-grade logging of Bedrock API calls and does not integrate with Bedrock’s native prompt management for template and model tracking.

options.text: Enable server access logging on S3 to record all interactions with stored prompts and summaries. Use AWS CloudTrail to log all API calls to Bedrock, and configure Bedrock’s Prompt Management service to oversee prompt lineage and model metadata.

correct_text: Enable server access logging on S3 to record all interactions with stored prompts and summaries. Use AWS CloudTrail to log all API calls to Bedrock, and configure Bedrock’s Prompt Management service to oversee prompt lineage and model metadata.
concepto: CloudTrail + Bedrock Prompt Management lineage

category: AIP – Operational Efficiency and Optimization for Generative AI Applications
stem: A banking institution plans to launch a generative AI (GenAI) solution built on Amazon Bedrock to empower customer support representatives with personalized financial guidance. To comply with industry regulations, the bank requires a governance and content safety architecture that aligns with responsible AI standards. The framework should incorporate proactive controls to screen for and block harmful content while also detecting and mitigating hallucinations in generated financial advice. The solution must also provide real-time monitoring of both model behavior and response drift, and maintain an immutable, audit-ready log of all prompt-response interactions for regulatory compliance. The institution must fulfill these requirements within a 60-day timeline, maintain end-to-end response latency below 200 ms, and provide seamless integration with existing internal compliance dashboards. Which approach satisfies these conditions with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Implement Bedrock guardrails as the core content safety framework to enforce safety thresholds and filter toxic content. Utilize Bedrock Model Evaluations to systematically assess response quality and uncover hallucinations. Log all prompt-response exchanges inside Amazon DynamoDB with a TTL policy for audit tracking. Emit custom metrics to Amazon CloudWatch to monitor model behavior and response drift, and feed this data into the existing compliance dashboard.

Develop custom AWS Lambda functions to evaluate outputs for accuracy and enforce content safety policies. Provision an Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor endpoint to track prediction quality and response drift in real time. Archive all prompt-response pairs into Amazon S3 to maintain regulatory audit trails. Export the S3 event logs to the compliance dashboard to monitor the operations.
options.rationale: because primarily relying on custom AWS Lambda functions to manually filter toxicity and check for accuracy introduces massive custom development overhead, making the 60-day deployment goal difficult. Additionally, invoking multiple Lambda functions synchronously will likely exceed the strict 200 ms latency requirement.

options.text: Implement Bedrock Agents combined with Bedrock Knowledge Base to ground responses and improve factual accuracy. Apply custom safety filters by training and deploying a dedicated Amazon SageMaker text classification model. Ingest all prompt-response records into Amazon OpenSearch Service for auditing. Connect OpenSearch Service to Amazon QuickSight to generate compliance reports.
options.rationale: because training, deploying, and maintaining a custom Amazon SageMaker text classification model specifically for safety filtering just introduces massive machine learning operational overhead compared to simply using native Amazon Bedrock guardrails. Additionally, deploying Amazon OpenSearch Service and building Amazon QuickSight dashboards introduces significantly more infrastructure management compared to using DynamoDB and CloudWatch.

options.text: Deploy AWS WAF ahead of Amazon API Gateway to filter incoming prompts for potential injection threats and apply rate limiting. Leverage Amazon Macie for ongoing analysis of AI-generated responses to detect hallucinations and monitor shifts in output behavior. Archive all prompt-response interactions within an Amazon RDS Multi-AZ deployments to facilitate regulatory audits. Integrate Amazon CloudWatch log streams with the compliance dashboard to enable real-time visibility into application health.
options.rationale: because while AWS WAF is highly effective for protecting API endpoints from common web exploits, it cannot semantically evaluate generative AI text payloads to enforce a comprehensive GenAI content safety framework. Additionally, Amazon Macie is a data security service built specifically to discover sensitive data (such as PII) within Amazon S3; it has no functionality to detect hallucinations or response drift in LLM outputs. Finally, establishing and maintaining an Amazon RDS relational database specifically for high-speed logging introduces unnecessary operational overhead and potential latency bottlenecks compared to Amazon DynamoDB.

correct_text: Implement Bedrock guardrails as the core content safety framework to enforce safety thresholds and filter toxic content. Utilize Bedrock Model Evaluations to systematically assess response quality and uncover hallucinations. Log all prompt-response exchanges inside Amazon DynamoDB with a TTL policy for audit tracking. Emit custom metrics to Amazon CloudWatch to monitor model behavior and response drift, and feed this data into the existing compliance dashboard.
concepto: Guardrails + Model Evaluations + drift monitoring GenAI

category: AIP – Foundation Model Integration, Data Management, and Compliance
stem: A fintech company is developing an AI-powered compliance assistant that performs a semantic search over a collection of regulatory documents to answer customer inquiries. The system must connect to Amazon Bedrock for natural language response generation. Document retrieval must function across three languages: English, Spanish, and Portuguese. The solution must support metadata-based filtering using fields such as issue date, governing authority, and document category. The underlying knowledge base contains approximately 10 million vector embeddings, requiring automated index optimization routines to sustain sub-second query performance without manual index tuning. The engineering team requires a fully managed approach to reduce the burden of infrastructure management. The solution must also return results with minimal latency to support real-time customer interactions. Which solution satisfies all of these requirements?

options.text: Configure Amazon OpenSearch Serverless as the vector store to handle semantic similarity searches and metadata-based filtering. Use Bedrock Knowledge Bases to establish a Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline backed by an Anthropic Claude foundation model (FM).

Launch an Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL cluster with the pgvector extension installed. Design relational schemas to persist vector embeddings alongside document metadata. Execute vector similarity queries through SQL. Route the retrieved documents to Bedrock to synthesize responses.
options.rationale: . While it can store and query vector embeddings alongside metadata, it primarily requires manual infrastructure management and fine-grained SQL query tuning. This contradicts the requirement to minimize operational overhead, and it is not a fully managed RAG solution when compared to the seamless integration that Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases provides with OpenSearch Serverless.

options.text: Set up Amazon Kendra as the enterprise document search engine. Enable metadata filtering using Kendra's attribute filter feature to scope results by governing authority, issue date, and document category. Connect retrieval results to Bedrock to generate final responses.
options.rationale: because Kendra is simply not a vector database and does not natively store or query vector embeddings at the scale of 10 million entries. It is designed for document-level enterprise search rather than embedding-level semantic similarity search, making it a poor fit for a RAG architecture that depends on dense vector retrieval with metadata filtering.

options.text: Provision Amazon MemoryDB with vector search support to store and query 10 million document embeddings. Apply metadata pre-filters during similarity queries to narrow the retrieval scope. Integrate the results with Bedrock to generate contextual responses for customer interactions.
options.rationale: . While MemoryDB supports vector search, its in-memory storage model is cost-inefficient and operationally complex for 10 million high-dimensional embeddings. It also lacks native integration with Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases, which means the fully managed RAG pipeline cannot be leveraged, contradicting the requirement to minimize management effort.

correct_text: Configure Amazon OpenSearch Serverless as the vector store to handle semantic similarity searches and metadata-based filtering. Use Bedrock Knowledge Bases to establish a Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline backed by an Anthropic Claude foundation model (FM).
concepto: OpenSearch Serverless vector store + Bedrock KB RAG

category: AIP – AI Safety, Security, and Governance
stem: A financial institution manages a centralized data lake on AWS Lake Formation, organizing sensitive transaction records and account data across multiple databases and tables to serve various business divisions and geographic regions. The organization plans to integrate an Amazon Bedrock foundation model (FM) to enhance its anti-money laundering (AML) detection capabilities. The FM requires access to financial records within the data lake, including certain datasets that contain customer personally identifiable information (PII), such as account holder names and identification numbers. To ensure compliance, the institution must establish a data access governance framework that masks PII fields at the column level and restricts the FM’s access to only authorized subsets of data. Additionally, all data access events must be logged and retained for regulatory audit purposes. Which of the following approaches fulfills these requirements?

options.text: Enable Amazon Macie to scan and classify PII across the data lake's Amazon S3 locations. Configure S3 access points with IAM role-based policies to serve pre-filtered data subsets to the Bedrock foundation model. Use S3 server access logging to retain records of all FM data retrieval requests.
options.rationale: because Amazon Macie is primarily a managed data security service that uses machine learning and pattern matching to discover and classify sensitive data, including PII, stored in Amazon S3; however, it identifies and reports where PII exists rather than enforcing column-level redaction at query time. S3 access points simplify access management for shared datasets but operate at the object level, not the column level, so there is no mechanism to mask specific PII fields before data reaches the foundation model. S3 server access logging also provides far less comprehensive auditing than AWS CloudTrail, which records all API-level data access events across integrated services. Most critically, this approach bypasses AWS Lake Formation entirely, which is the purpose-built service for enforcing column-level, attribute-based access governance in a data lake environment.

options.text: Create LF-Tags in Lake Formation to categorize resources by business division and geographic market, and apply these tags to the appropriate databases, tables, and columns. Use IAM roles to authenticate the Bedrock foundation model, enforcing Lake Formation permissions with LF-Tag expressions to ensure PII columns are excluded from the FM’s accessible data. Record all data access events using AWS CloudTrail.

Apply AWS Glue Data Quality rules to flag PII columns during ingestion. Use Glue Studio ETL jobs to redact sensitive fields and write sanitized outputs to a dedicated Amazon S3 prefix. Grant the Bedrock foundation model access to that prefix through IAM roles, and use Amazon CloudWatch Logs as the audit trail.
options.rationale: because AWS Glue Data Quality and Glue Studio ETL jobs simply apply column transformations at ingestion time, producing static sanitized copies of the data rather than enforcing dynamic, query-time access control. This means the institution must continuously maintain and synchronize a separate sanitized dataset alongside the source data, which introduces significant operational overhead. This approach also does not leverage AWS Lake Formation’s LF-Tag-based access model, which enforces column-level permissions natively across multiple business divisions and geographic markets without duplicating data. Additionally, Amazon CloudWatch Logs for Glue job runs capture ETL execution details but do not constitute a comprehensive data access audit trail.

options.text: Configure the Bedrock foundation model to assume an IAM role and request temporary credentials from AWS Security Token Service (STS). Use a middleware API to generate time-limited presigned Amazon S3 URLs with business division and regional filters applied. Log all data access activity using AWS CloudTrail.
options.rationale: because AWS Security Token Service (STS) is a service that issues temporary, limited-privilege credentials for IAM role assumption, commonly used for cross-account access or federated identity workflows, and presigned Amazon S3 URLs allow time-limited, credential-free access to specific S3 objects. Both mechanisms operate at the S3 object level, not at the column level, so there is no way to redact specific PII fields before data is delivered to the foundation model. The custom middleware API that generates presigned URLs adds operational complexity and introduces a point of failure that must be independently maintained and secured. While this option does correctly include AWS CloudTrail for auditing, the absence of AWS Lake Formation and LF-Tag-based column-level access control means the PII masking and fine-grained data subset enforcement requirements cannot be met.

correct_text: Create LF-Tags in Lake Formation to categorize resources by business division and geographic market, and apply these tags to the appropriate databases, tables, and columns. Use IAM roles to authenticate the Bedrock foundation model, enforcing Lake Formation permissions with LF-Tag expressions to ensure PII columns are excluded from the FM’s accessible data. Record all data access events using AWS CloudTrail.
concepto: Lake Formation LF-Tags column masking + CloudTrail

category: AIP – Operational Efficiency and Optimization for Generative AI Applications
stem: An organization is developing a generative AI-powered customer support assistant to answer complex inquiries and provide personalized product guidance. The assistant must retrieve relevant content from large volumes of structured and unstructured support data, including user manuals, help tickets, and technical notes. To enhance relevance and personalization, the team integrates Amazon Kendra to surface documents based on query intent and Amazon Personalize to recommend the most useful articles for individual customers based on historical interactions. The architecture must seamlessly integrate retrieval, personalization, and generative content generation to deliver accurate, timely responses at scale. The development team uses AWS CodeBuild to automate the assistant’s build and deployment pipelines. Which solution best meets these requirements?

options.text: Preprocess documents using Amazon Bedrock Model Customizations with semantic embeddings and prompt templates, and handle Kendra and Personalize ranking in separate pipelines.
options.rationale: . This approach only prepares embeddings and prompt templates without unifying retrieval, personalization, and RAG capabilities. Handling Kendra and Personalize in separate pipelines typically creates operational silos, increasing latency and making it harder to provide cohesive responses.

options.text: Build an Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base with hybrid search enabled. Enrich documents with Kendra metadata, and use Personalize to guide content retrieval and recommendations for the generative assistant.
Ingest and transform support content continuously with Amazon Bedrock Data Automation. Use Personalize to recommend content, and perform full-text search with Kendra independently.
options.rationale: . Using Bedrock Data Automation for ongoing ingestion improves data freshness, but it primarily solves ETL, not retrieval relevance. Running Personalize and Kendra independently means the system provides only standalone search and recommendation capabilities, without centralized orchestration for the generative assistant. Without Bedrock Knowledge Bases, hybrid search cannot be implemented natively, and the team would just be stitching together multiple systems manually, leading to higher latency and diminished ranking quality.

options.text: Orchestrate generative models with Amazon Bedrock Prompt Flows, then call Kendra and Personalize to rank or personalize outputs, and store results outside a centralized knowledge base.
options.rationale: . Bedrock Prompt Flows simply manages workflow logic and does not provide an integrated hybrid search or retrieval engine. Calling Kendra and Personalize separately outside of a centralized knowledge base typically leads to disconnected relevance scoring and inconsistent context for the generative model. Storing results outside a unified Knowledge Base only complicates long-term retrieval management and eliminates the benefits of hybrid search implementation.

correct_text: Build an Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base with hybrid search enabled. Enrich documents with Kendra metadata, and use Personalize to guide content retrieval and recommendations for the generative assistant.

category: AIP – AI Safety, Security, and Governance
stem: A financial services firm recently deployed an AI-powered customer support chatbot built on Amazon Bedrock. The chatbot handles inquiries related to account balances, transaction records, and billing history. As part of the firm’s regulatory obligations, data residency policies strictly prohibit AI inference across AWS Region boundaries; all model processing must occur within the same Region where a customer’s data is stored. Before the chatbot is made available to end users, the firm’s compliance team wants to run a structured evaluation to determine how reliably the chatbot identifies and suppresses personally identifiable information (PII) in its generated responses. Which of the following solutions fulfills these requirements?

options.text: Store all chatbot conversation logs in an Amazon S3 bucket with server-side encryption. Use Amazon Macie to automatically scan for PII, and set up an AWS Step Functions workflow to redact detected PII from flagged records before including them in compliance reports.
options.rationale: because Amazon S3 is an object storage service used for storing and retrieving data at scale, it is simply not designed to intercept or filter live model responses in real time. Amazon Macie is a data security service that uses machine learning to discover and classify sensitive data stored in S3 buckets, it operates on data at rest rather than on active model outputs. AWS Step Functions is a serverless workflow orchestration service used to coordinate multi-step automated pipelines, but introduces latency that makes it unsuitable as a real-time PII redaction layer. Because this approach only processes conversations after they are already stored, PII-containing responses may reach end users before any redaction occurs.

options.text: Set up a Bedrock Guardrail with sensitive information filters applied to both model inputs and outputs. Use mask mode during the evaluation phase to assess the effectiveness of PII suppression. Transition to block mode upon production release. Provision a dedicated guardrail instance in every AWS Region where the firm's customers are located.

Activate Bedrock Guardrails with sensitive information filters and set them to detect mode. Stream all flagged outputs to an Amazon Kinesis Data Stream for compliance review. Route outputs through an AWS Glue job to redact PII before delivering responses to customers in production.
options.rationale: because Amazon Kinesis Data Stream is a real-time data streaming service built for high-throughput event ingestion such as logs and telemetry — not for PII redaction in AI pipelines. AWS Glue is a serverless ETL service used to transform and prepare data for analytics workloads, and is not designed to serve as a real-time content filtering layer between a foundation model and an end user. Because Glue processes data asynchronously, PII-containing responses may still reach end users before any redaction takes place. Additionally, detect mode takes no corrective action on outputs, so no actual PII suppression occurs during testing or production.

options.text: Implement content and word filtering by configuring a cross-Region Bedrock guardrail. Begin with detect mode to monitor and log policy violations during evaluation, and transition to mask mode for enforcement in the production environment.
options.rationale: because content filters and word filters are designed to block harmful or restricted text categories and predefined phrases, they are simply not capable of detecting contextually sensitive personal information such as names, account numbers, or addresses. Sensitive information filters are the correct guardrail policy for PII suppression. Additionally, configuring a cross-Region guardrail contradicts the firm’s data residency policies, which require all model processing to remain within each customer’s local AWS Region. Using mask mode only in production also means the compliance team has no way to evaluate PII suppression effectiveness prior to launch.

correct_text: Set up a Bedrock Guardrail with sensitive information filters applied to both model inputs and outputs. Use mask mode during the evaluation phase to assess the effectiveness of PII suppression. Transition to block mode upon production release. Provision a dedicated guardrail instance in every AWS Region where the firm's customers are located.
concepto: Guardrails sensitive info filter mask/block por region

stem: A startup is building a customer-support chatbot using Amazon Bedrock foundation models. Users send messages via a REST API powered by Amazon API Gateway, which triggers an AWS Lambda function. The Lambda function calls the Bedrock InvokeModel API to generate responses. Separately, Amazon Comprehend is used to perform sentiment analysis on each user input before passing it to the Bedrock model. Recently, in production, the application started returning unexpected model outputs, but there is no visibility into which prompts are being sent to Bedrock or into the raw responses returned. A logging mechanism is required to debug, audit, and trace the full content of the prompts and the model’s completions for each Lambda-invoked Bedrock call, without modifying the business logic. Which approach is most effective for achieving this?

options.text: Add Amazon CloudWatch logging statements in the Lambda function to log the input message and the response that comes back from Bedrock’s InvokeModel API.
options.rationale: because it only captures what the Lambda function handles, not the exact content that Bedrock receives or returns. While it is helpful for basic debugging, it does not reliably record model-generated completions in their raw form. Therefore, it is simply insufficient for full auditing or tracing of prompts and responses.

options.text: Use AWS X-Ray to trace Lambda executions and identify performance issues or delays in calls to the Bedrock InvokeModel API.
options.rationale: . AWS X-Ray is primarily designed for performance monitoring, latency tracing, and identifying bottlenecks across services. It does not capture the raw content of prompts or model outputs. X-Ray can help understand timing issues, but is just a tool for observability, not for auditing model responses.

options.text: Enable Bedrock model invocation logging to capture the raw prompts and responses by configuring an InvocationLogsConfig that delivers logs to Amazon S3.
Route the InvokeModel requests through Amazon EventBridge to capture events and monitor model invocations for analysis.
options.rationale: . EventBridge captures event notifications and triggers downstream processes, but it typically only records metadata about requests, not the full request and response content. correct_text: Enable Bedrock model invocation logging to capture the raw prompts and responses by configuring an InvocationLogsConfig that delivers logs to Amazon S3.

stem: A large enterprise is building a conversational support agent that leverages Amazon SageMaker JumpStart to train custom embeddings from its internal knowledge base and uses Amazon Bedrock to power large‑language‑model responses. The application receives thousands of near‑duplicate semantic queries each day from customer service channels, and every invocation of the foundation model (FM) in Bedrock incurs significant costs and adds latency. The team wants to minimize repeated model calls by recognizing semantically similar queries that have been answered previously and serving cached responses quickly, while still allowing fresh model generation when truly new questions arrive. Which solution will meet this requirement?

options.text: Use an in‑memory key‑value store to cache exact request strings and responses, and only call the FM when the exact key is missing.
options.rationale: because it only supports exact string matching, which fails to recognize semantically similar queries phrased differently (e.g., “reset password” vs. “change login credentials”). This approach misses the opportunity to reuse responses for near-duplicate queries, leading to unnecessary FM invocations.

options.text: Pre‑compute embeddings with SageMaker AI, store them in a relational database, then query for an exact string match before invoking the FM.
options.rationale: because although it uses embeddings, it still relies on exact string matching in a relational database, which defeats the purpose of semantic similarity. Relational databases are not optimized for vector similarity search, and this setup would not reduce FM calls for semantically similar but differently worded queries.

options.text: Store query embeddings and responses in Amazon MemoryDB with vector search enabled, and implement semantic caching to return cached responses instead of invoking the FM.
Integrate Amazon Kendra to index all queries and their responses, and use Kendra’s search functionality to retrieve semantically similar queries before invoking the FM.
options.rationale: because Amazon Kendra is primarily designed for document and FAQ retrieval, not for low-latency, high-throughput semantic caching of conversational queries. It introduces unnecessary complexity and may not meet the performance and cost-efficiency needs of a real-time conversational agent.

correct_text: Store query embeddings and responses in Amazon MemoryDB with vector search enabled, and implement semantic caching to return cached responses instead of invoking the FM.
concepto: MemoryDB vector search para semantic caching

stem: A beverage company runs a mobile application that generates personalized drink formulation recommendations using Amazon Bedrock with a three-stage prompt chain. The prompt chain transforms customer health goals and flavor preferences into structured metadata, retrieves relevant historical formulation logs, and produces a tailored drink recommendation. Customers across several AWS Regions have experienced a range of issues: inconsistent formulation recommendations for identical inputs, high retrieval latency, and unsafe outputs – such as formulations with ingredient concentrations exceeding safe limits. To resolve these issues, the company must deploy validated safety controls to prevent hallucinated or unsafe recommendations, ensure output consistency of at least 99.5% for identical inputs, and decrease inference latency to less than one second. Which of the following solutions satisfies all of these specifications?

options.text: Enable Bedrock provisioned throughput to ensure consistent inference latency across all Regions. Implement Bedrock Guardrails with semantic denial rules to block unsafe prompts from unsafe formulations. Utilize Bedrock Prompt Management with approval workflows to govern, version, and control all prompt chain templates.

Run Bedrock model evaluation jobs to assess output consistency across all three stages of the prompt chain. Deploy a secondary validation model on an Amazon SageMaker real-time endpoint to screen recommendations before delivery. Configure Amazon CloudWatch alarms to trigger automated rollbacks when output inconsistency is detected.
options.rationale: because Amazon Bedrock model evaluation jobs primarily measure the quality of model outputs in a batch, offline fashion, and are not designed to enforce real-time output consistency for live inference calls. They evaluate past outputs instead of ensuring 99.5% consistency for identical new inputs. Using a secondary validation model on Amazon SageMaker increases operational overhead and latency without providing the same validated safety controls as Amazon Bedrock Guardrails with semantic denial rules. While Amazon CloudWatch alarms can trigger reactive responses to threshold breaches, automated rollbacks are not preventive—by the time an alarm is triggered, inconsistent or unsafe recommendations may already have reached customers.

options.text: Cache prompt outputs for repeated formulation inputs in Amazon ElastiCache to reduce inference calls. Use AWS Lambda to pre-process customer preference inputs before each stage of the prompt chain. Integrate AWS X-Ray into the application to monitor end-to-end latency and pinpoint bottlenecks within the retrieval process.
options.rationale: because Amazon ElastiCache caching reduces inference calls only for inputs that have been seen before and are cache-eligible, but it cannot guarantee 99.5% output consistency for the full range of unique input combinations that the three-stage prompt chain encounters. AWS Lambda pre-processing adds an extra invocation step to each stage, which can increase rather than decrease end-to-end latency when the retrieval stage is already the bottleneck. AWS X-Ray is a distributed tracing service that identifies performance bottlenecks but does not resolve them, it just provides observability without remediation. Most critically, none of these services provide validated safety controls to block unsafe or hallucinated formulation recommendations.

options.text: Apply prompt compression to the three-stage prompt chain to reduce token usage and improve retrieval stage throughput. Use Bedrock Agents to orchestrate and manage outputs across each stage of the chain. Use Amazon Comprehend to detect and flag formulations that exceed safe ingredient concentration thresholds before delivering recommendations.
options.rationale: because prompt compression reduces the number of tokens sent to the model per invocation, which can lower costs and improve latency for token-heavy prompts, but it does not enforce output consistency. Even with identical compressed prompts, outputs may vary without proper versioning or governance. While Amazon Bedrock Agents orchestrate multi-step workflows with tool use and memory, they do not resolve the core issue of inconsistent outputs—the lack of governed, versioned prompt templates that Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management offers. Amazon Comprehend, though useful for extracting entities and sentiment, is not a validated safety control for blocking hallucinated or unsafe GenAI outputs; this function requires Amazon Bedrock Guardrails with semantic denial rules.

correct_text: Enable Bedrock provisioned throughput to ensure consistent inference latency across all Regions. Implement Bedrock Guardrails with semantic denial rules to block unsafe prompts from unsafe formulations. Utilize Bedrock Prompt Management with approval workflows to govern, version, and control all prompt chain templates.
concepto: Provisioned throughput + Guardrails + Prompt Management

stem: A large industrial‑equipment provider has built an operational expert system using Amazon SageMaker AI to generate embeddings from service‑log text and document archives, and uses Amazon Bedrock to deliver answers via a foundation‑model interface. The provider stores millions of maintenance and fault‑analysis records and requires semantic retrieval of relevant content plus metadata filtering (equipment type, date, severity) for rapid context delivery into the Bedrock prompt. The team needs to choose a vector store that supports efficient embedding loading, high‑speed approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search, and direct integration with the relational metadata environment. Which solution will meet this requirement for deploying and configuring the vector search infrastructure?

options.text: Configure pgvector extension inside Amazon Aurora (PostgreSQL Compatible). options.rationale: because while OpenSearch primarily supports vector search, its metadata filtering is less expressive and performant than SQL joins. It lacks tight relational integration, which is critical for complex filtering on structured metadata like equipment type, date, and severity.

options.text: Deploy a PostgreSQL database with embeddings stored as arrays or JSON, use user‑defined functions (UDFs) to compute cosine similarity at runtime, join with metadata, and invoke retrieval from Bedrock.
options.rationale: because storing embeddings as arrays or JSON and computing similarity via UDFs is inefficient and does not scale well. It lacks ANN indexing, leading to poor performance on large datasets with millions of records.

options.text: Use SageMaker Feature Store to store embeddings and metadata, then at query time, invoke a SageMaker real‑time endpoint to compute the nearest neighbors with embedded logic, then pass the results to Bedrock.
options.rationale: because SageMaker Feature Store is not typically optimized for vector similarity search. Using real-time inference for nearest-neighbor search introduces latency and complexity, making it unsuitable for high-speed retrieval at scale

stem: A media streaming company runs a personalized content recommendation engine on Amazon EC2 instances. Each instance mounts an Amazon EBS volume that stores a local cache of pre-computed customer preference vectors, which the application reads at query time to enrich prompts before calling Amazon Bedrock foundation models for final recommendation scoring. The engineering team has observed intermittent periods in which recommendation quality degrades, and customers receive off-target suggestions, but the team cannot determine whether the root cause is EBS I/O latency starving the feature retrieval pipeline or FM behavioral drift in the Bedrock model responses. The company needs an observability solution that automatically discovers and monitors both the EC2 compute layer and the attached EBS volumes as a unified application stack, detects performance deviations from established baselines using historical patterns rather than static thresholds, and generates correlated alerts within 10 minutes when anomalies are detected across any layer of the stack. The solution must minimize the effort required for manual monitoring configuration. Which solution satisfies these requirements?

options.text: Enable Amazon CloudWatch Container Insights on the EC2 instances. Configure Container Insights to collect CPU, memory, and disk I/O metrics at the instance level. Set CloudWatch alarms on Container Insights metrics with static latency thresholds to alert when EBS read latency exceeds a defined limit.
options.rationale: because it is primarily designed for containerized workloads on ECS, EKS, and Kubernetes platforms, not for standalone EC2 and EBS application stacks. It does not monitor EBS volume performance metrics, does not integrate FM invocation telemetry, and does not provide ML-powered cross-layer anomaly detection and automated correlation dashboards like Application Insights.

options.text: Enable Amazon CloudWatch Application Insights on the resource group containing the EC2 instances and attached EBS volumes. Configure custom recommendation quality metrics using the embedded metric format with dimensions for customer segment and FM model ID. Use Application Insights' ML-powered anomaly detection to automatically baseline performance patterns across the EC2, EBS, and FM metric layers and generate correlated alerts when deviations are detected.

Deploy AWS X-Ray tracing across the EC2 application processes. Route trace segments to Amazon Data Firehose and deliver them to Amazon QuickSight. Build custom QuickSight dashboards with manually configured alert rules to monitor EBS read latency trends and FM response times.
options.rationale: because X-Ray does not perform ML-powered anomaly detection, and the QuickSight pipeline imposes substantial manual build and maintenance overhead. The architecture simply cannot automatically correlate EBS I/O anomalies with FM behavioral deviations or trigger alerts within 10 minutes based on dynamic baselines.

options.text: Provision an Amazon OpenSearch Service cluster with the Observability plugin. Configure Amazon Data Firehose to ingest Amazon CloudWatch metrics for EC2 and EBS alongside Bedrock invocation logs. Write custom OpenSearch anomaly detectors and alerting rules to surface multi-layer performance correlations.
options.rationale: because it only introduces high ongoing operational overhead for cluster provisioning, index management, and custom anomaly rule authoring that directly contradicts the requirement to minimize manual configuration effort. The same outcome can be achieved natively in CloudWatch Application Insights with significantly less setup.

correct_text: Enable Amazon CloudWatch Application Insights on the resource group containing the EC2 instances and attached EBS volumes. Configure custom recommendation quality metrics using the embedded metric format with dimensions for customer segment and FM model ID. Use Application Insights' ML-powered anomaly detection to automatically baseline performance patterns across the EC2, EBS, and FM metric layers and generate correlated alerts when deviations are detected.

stem: A medical enterprise utilizes an Amazon Bedrock application to summarize patient records. However, the system suffers from intermittent output degradation, specifically generating factual hallucinations. The operational expenses have surpassed the monthly budget by 40%. A GenAI Engineer needs a near-real-time observability strategy to uncover these factual hallucinations, monitor the utilization of the system’s token processing capacity, and issue early alerts for unexpected cost spikes. The chosen architecture must minimize custom scripting and ongoing operational burden. Which solution satisfies these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Deploy Amazon CloudWatch alarms to monitor InputTokenCount and OutputTokenCount for anomalous token usage. Route all model invocation logs to Amazon S3 with automated text output capture. Integrate AWS Glue and Amazon Athena to perform scalable, on-demand analysis across these logs, enabling the identification of factual hallucinations in near real time.
options.rationale: because building ETL (Extract, Transform, Load) pipelines with AWS Glue to process logs and querying them via Amazon Athena is an asynchronous, batch-oriented process. This approach is excellent for historical analytics but fundamentally fails to provide the near-real-time hallucination detection required by the scenario. Furthermore, writing and maintaining custom SQL queries and ETL scripts introduces significant custom development and maintenance overhead compared to simply enabling native guardrails. Lastly, standard CloudWatch alarms often rely on static thresholds, which are not as adaptive or accurate as machine learning-powered anomaly detection for catching unpredictable spikes in token usage.

options.text: Configure Bedrock Model Evaluation to run continuous automated jobs to spot factual hallucinations. Stream the model invocation logs into Amazon CloudWatch Logs and use CloudWatch Logs Insights to build queries that detect spikes in token utilization.
options.rationale: because Amazon Bedrock Model Evaluation is primarily designed for point-in-time benchmarking and comparing different foundation models against curated datasets prior to deployment. It is not designed for near-real-time, inline hallucination detection during live application inference. Furthermore, while CloudWatch Logs Insights is a powerful tool for ad-hoc log analysis, relying on it means developers must manually run queries or set up complex scheduled query mechanisms, which fails to provide the robust, automated early warnings natively offered by CloudWatch alarms.

options.text: Enable Bedrock to export model invocation logs, with text output logging activated, directly to Amazon S3 for centralized storage and analysis. Apply Bedrock guardrails leveraging contextual grounding checks to automatically detect and flag factual inaccuracies in model outputs. Deploy Amazon CloudWatch anomaly detection alarms to continuously monitor token usage metrics and generate real-time alerts upon detecting abnormal patterns.

Deploy a Bedrock agent configured with an AWS Lambda Action Group to dynamically validate outputs for factual hallucinations. Export the model invocation logs to Amazon OpenSearch Service and configure OpenSearch alerts to detect deviations in token processing capacity.
options.rationale: because relying on an AWS Lambda function to dynamically validate outputs means writing, deploying, and maintaining custom validation logic or secondary prompt chains. This drastically increases the custom development burden, introduces additional latency to the medical application, and is far more complex than natively enabling contextual grounding. Moreover, exporting logs to Amazon OpenSearch Service and configuring its alerting mechanisms introduces unnecessary infrastructure deployment, cluster scaling, and management overhead just to monitor token metrics—a task that native CloudWatch handles with zero additional infrastructure.

correct_text: Enable Bedrock to export model invocation logs, with text output logging activated, directly to Amazon S3 for centralized storage and analysis. Apply Bedrock guardrails leveraging contextual grounding checks to automatically detect and flag factual inaccuracies in model outputs. Deploy Amazon CloudWatch anomaly detection alarms to continuously monitor token usage metrics and generate real-time alerts upon detecting abnormal patterns.

stem: An organization is scaling GenAI workloads to generate real-time insights from economic filings, market sentiment reports, and regulatory disclosures. The pipeline uses Amazon Titan Embeddings for vectorizing textual data and Amazon Rekognition to extract features from financial charts. After preprocessing, the inputs are routed to a foundation model (FM) in Amazon Bedrock. Internal telemetry reveals that many FM invocations come from recurring workflows with prompts that are phrased differently but express the same underlying intent, leading to cost overruns and latency spikes that impact downstream systems requiring fast model responses. To address this issue, the architecture team must implement a caching strategy that avoids redundant FM calls for prompts that convey the same meaning, even if the phrasing differs. The solution must support multi-region workloads, generate consistent cache keys, and ensure reliable cached outputs for subsequent GenAI operations. The selected approach must directly optimize cost, latency, and response consistency across highly distributed GenAI pipelines handling both structured and unstructured financial data. Which strategy best meets these requirements?

options.text: Implement deterministic request hashing by generating unique, repeatable hashes from the content of incoming prompts.
options.rationale: because deterministic request hashing relies on generating a hash based on the exact or minimal variation in the prompt text, which is not effective for semantically similar prompts that differ slightly in wording. This approach typically only works for prompts that are almost identical or share a very similar structure, and therefore, it would fail to recognize prompts that are semantically equivalent but phrased differently, making it unsuitable for the current scenario where slight variations in phrasing need to be handled.

options.text: Implement semantic caching that matches semantically similar prompts and reuses model outputs.
Implement edge caching to store FM outputs at geographically distributed edge locations.
options.rationale: because edge caching is focused on improving performance by serving cached results closer to the user, reducing latency for distant requests. However, this approach primarily addresses geographic distribution and does not solve the issue of repeated FM invocations for semantically similar prompts. It does not help with reducing the need for redundant model calls when the prompts are not identical, which is the core problem in this scenario.

options.text: Implement prompt caching by storing each exact prompt and its corresponding output.
options.rationale: because prompt caching stores exact matches of prompts and their corresponding outputs, only serving the cached result when an identical prompt is encountered. This method simply does not work for scenarios where prompts differ slightly in phrasing but ask for the same or semantically similar insight. It would not be able to handle the variations in wording described in the scenario, making it ineffective for reducing redundant model invocations.

correct_text: Implement semantic caching that matches semantically similar prompts and reuses model outputs.

options.rationale: because Amazon Comprehend is not designed for FM hallucination grounding checks, and an EventBridge-to-SNS pipeline without anomaly detection cannot distinguish normal usage patterns from genuine cost anomalies or injection-driven token spikes.

options.text: Enable Bedrock model invocation logging with text output and store logs in Amazon S3. correct_text: Enable Bedrock model invocation logging with text output and store logs in Amazon S3. stem: An organization is developing an AI-powered customer support assistant that leverages Amazon Bedrock for providing real-time responses to customer queries. The assistant must fetch product details from an organization’s backend infrastructure, available only via a secure REST API. This API requires authentication with an API key that expires every 30 minutes and must be refreshed regularly. To maintain secure, seamless access to the API, the company needs to fetch a new API key from an OAuth provider dynamically. The entire solution should be integrated into an Amazon API Gateway method that ensures secure API access, manages token updates, and provides low latency for real-time customer interactions. What is the best approach to meet these requirements?

options.text: Configure the Amazon API Gateway to integrate with AWS Lambda using an API proxy integration. The Lambda function will authenticate via the OAuth provider, retrieve a fresh token, and pass it as a header to the Bedrock agent to make the API call to the external system.
options.rationale: because Lambda proxy integrations are primarily used for forwarding requests to backend services, not for managing dynamic token generation and interacting with the agent. The token generation and external API call should be managed by a dedicated Lambda function in the agent’s action group, which is better suited for real-time, low-latency requirements. Using a proxy integration in this case unnecessarily complicates the flow and introduces additional layers of abstraction.

options.text: Set up a custom AWS Lambda function integrated with Amazon API Gateway that handles the OAuth token generation for API access. The Lambda function will request a fresh token from the OAuth provider and inject it as a custom header for the Bedrock agent. The API Gateway method will invoke the Lambda function, passing the request and token to the agent for further processing.
options.rationale: because this option mixes the token management logic with the agent’s core request flow. Although it does use Lambda to generate the token, it fails to fully separate concerns as it combines the token generation and API interaction within a single Lambda function, reducing scalability and flexibility. The proper design involves keeping the Lambda function focused on managing the token and external API call, and the InvokeAgent API for direct communication.

options.text: Use Amazon CloudFront to cache OAuth credentials and API tokens. Configure an AWS Lambda function that fetches the token from CloudFront’s cache and makes the external API call. The API Gateway method will invoke the Lambda function to retrieve the cached token from CloudFront and pass it to the Bedrock agent for processing.
options.rationale: because CloudFront is not designed for securely caching dynamic tokens like OAuth credentials. CloudFront is only intended for caching static content, such as images or videos, not sensitive data. Caching tokens in CloudFront could expose security vulnerabilities and introduce latency in retrieving the tokens.

options.text: Develop an AWS Lambda function for the Bedrock agent action group that handles OAuth token generation and calls the external REST API. Set up the API Gateway method to utilize the Bedrock InvokeAgent API for communication with the agent. Ensure the appropriate IAM permissions are granted to allow the API Gateway to trigger the Bedrock agent.

correct_text: Develop an AWS Lambda function for the Bedrock agent action group that handles OAuth token generation and calls the external REST API. Set up the API Gateway method to utilize the Bedrock InvokeAgent API for communication with the agent.
