stem: A financial services company is building an AI assistant using Amazon Bedrock to help clients manage investment portfolios. The assistant leverages the foundation models (FMs) available within Bedrock to handle complex queries related to stock performance, market trends, and risk assessments. The setup also includes Amazon Polly to provide text-to-speech responses, allowing users to hear immediate updates as the assistant handles client interactions. The assistant currently processes each request in full before providing any feedback, resulting in significant delays that negatively affect the user experience. To improve satisfaction, the company wants to deliver partial insights or preliminary responses while the assistant continues processing, enabling users to receive timely feedback without waiting for the full analysis to complete. Which solution will meet these objectives while minimizing development effort?

options.text: Create an HTTP API with Amazon API Gateway and AWS Lambda. Use AWS Step Functions to manage parallel processing and store partial results in Amazon DynamoDB. Set up a DynamoDB Stream to trigger a Lambda function that sends real-time updates to the client when data changes.
options.rationale: because Step Functions are primarily designed for orchestrating workflows and managing long-running, multi-step tasks. While they can handle parallel processing, they introduce additional complexity and potential delays in providing real-time feedback, which is not ideal for a use case that requires immediate updates. Using DynamoDB Streams with Lambda can provide updates, but polling or event-driven triggers still do not meet the need for real-time feedback during the analysis, as required by the scenario.

options.text: Set up a WebSocket API with Amazon API Gateway and AWS Lambda. Use the InvokeModelWithResponseStream API from Bedrock to stream results to clients via WebSockets. Implement a Lambda function to handle connections and deliver messages dynamically.

Set up a REST API with Amazon API Gateway and AWS Lambda. Use the InvokeModel API from Bedrock to process requests sequentially and store responses in Amazon S3. Implement client-side polling with JavaScript’s setInterval to check for updates in S3.
options.rationale: because using a REST API and InvokeModel API processes requests sequentially, which introduces delays and doesn’t provide real-time feedback. This means the assistant would have to wait for the full analysis to complete before responding, which is inefficient. Additionally, client-side polling introduces more latency by requiring periodic checks for updates, and Amazon S3 is not optimized for real-time data streaming.

options.text: Deploy a real-time API with AWS AppSync using AWS Lambda resolvers. Set up a GraphQL schema to stream data, and use Bedrock’s InvokeModel API to handle model responses while using subscriptions to update clients in real-time.
options.rationale: because AWS AppSync is primarily intended for managing structured data and real-time communication with GraphQL. While subscriptions work for certain real-time updates, the use of GraphQL can add unnecessary complexity when compared to simpler solutions like WebSockets for real-time communication. Moreover, AppSync typically introduces overhead that may not be necessary for a straightforward streaming solution, where WebSockets offer a more efficient and direct method for streaming real-time data between clients and the server.

correct_text: Set up a WebSocket API with Amazon API Gateway and AWS Lambda. Use the InvokeModelWithResponseStream API from Bedrock to stream results to clients via WebSockets. Implement a Lambda function to handle connections and deliver messages dynamically.
concepto: InvokeModelWithResponseStream sobre WebSocket API

category: AIP – AI Safety, Security, and Governance
stem: An e-commerce business recently launched an AI-powered customer support portal, powered by an Amazon Bedrock Foundation Model (FM), to handle the growing volume of customer inquiries. The portal processes customer-submitted messages, extracts key concerns, and generates draft responses for agent review. As part of its responsible AI framework, the business wants to introduce a multi-layered content filtering pipeline powered by Amazon Comprehend to screen all incoming messages before those messages are passed to the FM. The filtering pipeline must address three specific requirements: it must detect and suppress offensive or harmful language, it must identify and redact any personally identifiable information (PII) to comply with customer data privacy policies, and it must flag messages that solicit inappropriate advice, including those that encourage fraudulent activity, unethical conduct, or manipulative behavior toward other customers. To avoid degrading the customer experience, the entire filtering pipeline must complete within the pre-processing stage and must not introduce delays that would push filtering beyond the point of FM invocation. Which of the following architectures will achieve these requirements?

options.text: Run all filtering operations concurrently using asynchronous API calls. Apply toxicity detection to flag and block offensive language. Use prompt safety classification to identify solicitations for inappropriate advice. Enable PII detection with entity redaction to protect customer privacy before content reaches the Bedrock FM.
options.rationale: because this option simply does not define calibrated detection thresholds for the toxicity detection layer. Without explicitly setting a threshold, such as 0.5 across all offense categories, the filtering pipeline simply lacks the precision needed to consistently suppress harmful content at an appropriate sensitivity level. Additionally, this option omits any mechanism for monitoring filtering pipeline performance, such as Amazon CloudWatch alarms, which are necessary to ensure the pre-processing stage consistently completes within acceptable response times under varying production loads.

options.text: Set up an AWS Lambda function to evaluate each incoming message against a predefined blocklist stored in Amazon DynamoDB. If the message passes the blocklist check, invoke Comprehend toxicity detection to screen for offensive content. Forward only clean messages to the Bedrock FM and log all flagged interactions to Amazon S3 for compliance review.
options.rationale: because a static blocklist stored in Amazon DynamoDB cannot dynamically detect nuanced offensive content, evolving inappropriate advice patterns, or personally identifiable information, all of which require the semantic understanding that Amazon Comprehend’s machine learning-based detectors provide. This option also omits PII detection and redaction entirely, leaving customer data privacy obligations unaddressed. Furthermore, primarily applying toxicity detection sequentially after a blocklist check introduces unnecessary latency into the pre-processing pipeline, which conflicts with the requirement that all filtering must complete before FM invocation without degrading the customer experience.

options.text: Configure an Amazon SQS queue to buffer all incoming customer messages before processing. Invoke an AWS Lambda function to call the Comprehend PII detection on each message and store redacted versions in Amazon S3. Use Bedrock Guardrails to apply topic filters for inappropriate advice before routing the message to the FM for response generation.
options.rationale: because introducing an Amazon SQS queue adds asynchronous queuing latency to the pipeline, which directly conflicts with the requirement that the entire filtering stage must complete within the pre-processing window before content reaches the FM. Additionally, applying Amazon Bedrock Guardrails as the mechanism for flagging inappropriate advice means the filtering occurs at the model boundary rather than as an upstream pre-processing step, violating the layered filtering architecture the scenario requires. This option also lacks toxicity detection entirely, leaving offensive or harmful language unaddressed in the pipeline.

options.text: Activate toxicity detection and set detection thresholds to 0.5 across all offense categories. Execute prompt safety classification and PII detection with entity redaction simultaneously through parallel processing. Monitor all filtering pipeline metrics and configure Amazon CloudWatch alarms to alert on threshold breaches before content is forwarded to the Bedrock FM.

correct_text: Activate toxicity detection and set detection thresholds to 0.5 across all offense categories. Execute prompt safety classification and PII detection with entity redaction simultaneously through parallel processing. Monitor all filtering pipeline metrics and configure Amazon CloudWatch alarms to alert on threshold breaches before content is forwarded to the Bedrock FM.
concepto: Comprehend toxicity + PII redaction + prompt safety

category: AIP – Operational Efficiency and Optimization for Generative AI Applications
stem: A global retail company is transforming its customer support system with a conversational AI chatbot built using Amazon Lex for natural language understanding and automated conversation flows. Amazon Transcribe is integrated for speech-to-text conversion, allowing customers to voice inquiries and interact naturally with the system. This setup improves the customer experience by enabling spoken communication, but the company now aims to automate the chatbot’s responses by leveraging its vast knowledge base of product documentation, FAQs, and support articles. The solution must quickly and accurately retrieve relevant information from the company’s documentation library. It should seamlessly integrate with existing AWS tools to provide real-time, dynamic responses to customer queries, reducing the need for manual updates or custom model training. What approach will provide the desired result with the least amount of development work?

options.text: Train a Bidirectional Attention Flow (BiDAF) model using customer questions and company documentation, deploy it via Amazon SageMaker AI, and integrate it with the chatbot through the SageMaker Runtime InvokeEndpoint API to provide responses.
options.rationale: because it requires significant custom development for model training and deployment. Custom model training using SageMaker typically involves complex processes like data preparation, feature engineering, and optimization, which increases the overall development effort compared to using a service like Amazon Kendra, which is designed for document search and retrieval with minimal setup. Also, while Bedrock Knowledge Base is useful for managing knowledge and leveraging large language models (LLMs), it is not designed for storing and indexing large volumes of unstructured documentation.

options.text: Store the company documentation in an Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base, then use Amazon Comprehend to analyze the customer queries and extract relevant insights from the documentation to provide accurate responses.
options.rationale: because Amazon Comprehend is primarily used for text analysis, such as sentiment detection or entity extraction, rather than for document retrieval. Using Comprehend to extract insights would require manual intervention to link it to the chatbot and is simply less efficient than using Amazon Kendra, which is specifically designed for document indexing and search, providing more accurate results for dynamic query answering.

options.text: Utilize Amazon Kendra for indexing company documents and integrate it with the chatbot through the Kendra Query API for dynamic response generation.
Use a BERT-based model in Amazon SageMaker AI, store documentation in Amazon S3, and rely on Lex to handle queries and invoke the SageMaker endpoint for responses.
options.rationale: because this approach involves building and training a custom BERT-based model, which requires significant time and expertise. Simply storing documentation in S3 and using SageMaker for inference introduces unnecessary complexity compared to using Amazon Kendra, which can index documents directly and provide relevant answers through a more efficient API, without the need for custom model training.

correct_text: Utilize Amazon Kendra for indexing company documents and integrate it with the chatbot through the Kendra Query API for dynamic response generation.
concepto: Amazon Kendra Query API para respuestas de chatbot

category: AIP – AI Safety, Security, and Governance
stem: A digital marketing agency uses Amazon Bedrock and Amazon SageMaker AI to generate personalized content for clients across various industries. The agency recently conducted an architecture review using the AWS WA Tool Generative AI Lens to evaluate its generative AI workloads against best practices. The agency requires a solution within Bedrock Prompt Management that enables the creation and maintenance of reusable, parameterized prompt templates. These templates must accommodate client-specific customizations, such as tone, product features, and promotional guidelines. Additionally, the agency needs to enforce strict style rules, such as tone restrictions and keyword exclusions, to ensure consistency across all content. The company also needs to track template usage and changes for compliance purposes, ensuring that updates to prompt templates go through a formal review and approval process before activation. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Configure reusable templates with client-specific parameters and versioning, and establish a formal review process for template updates. Apply Bedrock Guardrails to enforce style rules, and use Amazon CloudWatch to monitor and log template usage and modifications.
options.rationale: because Amazon CloudWatch is typically designed for operational metrics and performance monitoring, not for detailed audit trails. It lacks the granularity and compliance focus that AWS CloudTrail provides.

options.text: Enable Bedrock Guardrails to automatically ensure templates meet style guidelines, and integrate AWS CloudTrail to capture detailed logs of prompt usage and template changes. Implement versioning to manage updates efficiently.
options.rationale: because it does not mention a formal review and approval process for template updates. Without this governance step, the solution would not meet the compliance requirement for controlled activation of changes.

options.text: Configure reusable templates with client-specific parameters and versioning, and establish a formal review process for template updates. Apply Bedrock Guardrails to enforce style rules, and use AWS CloudTrail to track template modifications and usage for compliance.

Develop parameterized templates in Bedrock Prompt Management with versioning, then use Amazon Comprehend to enforce style rules for tone and keywords. Use AWS CloudTrail to monitor template changes and usage.
options.rationale: because Amazon Comprehend is not primarily designed to enforce style rules. It can analyze tone and sentiment, but cannot apply restrictions or exclusions. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails is the correct tool for enforcing tone, keyword exclusions, and other stylistic constraints.

correct_text: Configure reusable templates with client-specific parameters and versioning, and establish a formal review process for template updates. Apply Bedrock Guardrails to enforce style rules, and use AWS CloudTrail to track template modifications and usage for compliance.
concepto: Prompt Management parametrizado + Guardrails + CloudTrail

category: AIP – AI Safety, Security, and Governance
stem: A pharmaceutical research firm has integrated clinical trial documentation into an AI assistant powered by an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base. The documentation contains sensitive patient data, and the firm must ensure that personally identifiable information (PII) is visible only to authorized medical researchers, while compliance auditors interacting with the same assistant must receive responses with all PII automatically redacted. The AI assistant must only draw from clinical documents published within the last 3 years. Reports are uploaded to an Amazon S3 bucket upon completion, and Amazon Cognito is used to manage and authenticate user identities. Which approach satisfies these requirements?

options.text: Configure an AWS Lambda function to automatically invoke Amazon Rekognition whenever a new document is uploaded, scanning each file for sensitive patient identifiers. Provision separate Bedrock knowledge bases for each user role, and dynamically route users to the appropriate knowledge base based on their Cognito group. Implement an S3 Lifecycle policy for the bucket to automatically delete documents older than 3 years.
options.rationale: because Amazon Rekognition is primarily a cloud-based computer vision service designed to analyze visual media such as images and videos, including object detection, facial recognition, and scene classification. It has no capability to identify or redact PII entities within text-based clinical documents such as PDFs or structured reports. Furthermore, provisioning separate knowledge bases for each user role and managing routing logic introduces significant operational overhead. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails with the ApplyGuardrail API already provides a built-in, role-aware mechanism to selectively redact PII at response time without duplicating the knowledge base infrastructure.

options.text: Deploy a Bedrock agent with an action group that invokes an AWS Lambda function on each user query. Configure the Lambda function to retrieve the user's Cognito group and call Amazon Comprehend to detect and redact PII from the response before returning it to the user. Apply an S3 Lifecycle configuration to remove documents older than 3 years.
options.rationale: because Amazon Comprehend is a natural language processing (NLP) service capable of detecting PII entity types such as names, dates, and medical record numbers within unstructured text. While it can be paired with AWS Lambda to programmatically scan and redact sensitive content, invoking this custom pipeline on every single user query simply introduces unnecessary latency and operational complexity. This approach duplicates functionality that Amazon Bedrock Guardrails already provides natively.

options.text: Apply an S3 Lifecycle rule on the source bucket to expire documents that exceed the 3-year retention period. Set up a scheduled AWS Lambda function to run periodic synchronization jobs between the S3 bucket and Bedrock knowledge base. For every user session, determine the authenticated user’s Cognito group and invoke the ApplyGuardrail

Enforce a 3-year document retention window by attaching an S3 Lifecycle configuration to the source bucket. Each time a new file lands in the bucket, have an AWS Lambda function push its contents to the primary Bedrock knowledge base. Before loading documents into a separate secondary knowledge base, run them via Amazon Comprehend to strip any detected PII. When a query arrives, check the user's Cognito group and direct the request to the full or redacted knowledge base accordingly.
options.rationale: because Amazon Bedrock knowledge bases allow organizations to connect foundation models to private data sources, enabling retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) workflows. While it is technically possible to provision multiple knowledge bases from the same S3 data source, maintaining two parallel knowledge bases — one with full PII and one with pre-redacted content — doubles the infrastructure footprint, synchronization complexity, and ongoing maintenance burden. Any update to a source document would require re-syncing both knowledge bases independently. Additionally, pre-redacting content at ingestion time permanently removes PII context from the redacted knowledge base, limiting future flexibility.

correct_text: Apply an S3 Lifecycle rule on the source bucket to expire documents that exceed the 3-year retention period. Set up a scheduled AWS Lambda function to run periodic synchronization jobs between the S3 bucket and Bedrock knowledge base. For every user session, determine the authenticated user’s Cognito group and invoke the ApplyGuardrail
concepto: ApplyGuardrail por grupo Cognito + KB sync + S3 lifecycle

stem: A firm utilizes Amazon SageMaker AI for building credit‑risk models and Amazon Rekognition for validating identity documents submitted by customers. The organization now seeks to deploy a fully autonomous investigation agent. Whenever a flagged account transaction occurs, the agent must trigger the risk‑model inference in SageMaker AI, retrieve relevant identity‑verification images from Rekognition, call internal APIs to gather customer data, and decide whether to escalate the case for manual review or automatically close the account. The solution needs to integrate seamlessly with AWS services, allow for custom tool integrations, and support the selection of multiple foundation models for reasoning and decision‑making. Which solution will meet this requirement in the most appropriate way?

options.text: Use Amazon Bedrock Agents with predefined action groups for SageMaker AI and Rekognition, and let the agent orchestrate all steps.
options.rationale: because Bedrock Agents currently support limited predefined action groups and lack full flexibility for integrating custom internal APIs or dynamically selecting among multiple foundation models. This restricts the agent’s ability to perform complex, multi-step investigations with custom logic.

options.text: Use AWS Strands Agents SDK to build a custom autonomous agent, integrating SageMaker AI, Rekognition, internal APIs, and selecting a foundation model via Amazon Bedrock.
Use a Lambda‑based orchestrator with AWS Step Functions that sequentially calls SageMaker, Rekognition, and internal APIs, and then uses a simple rule engine for escalation logic.
options.rationale: because while this solution typically handles orchestration, it lacks autonomous reasoning. A rule engine is static and cannot adapt or reason like a foundation model. This approach doesn’t meet the requirement for intelligent decision-making or model selection.

options.text: Use SageMaker AI Pipelines that execute the model inference and Rekognition check as steps, and then embed a causal chain prompting strategy within the model for decision making.
options.rationale: because SageMaker Pipelines are primarily designed for ML workflows, not for orchestrating multi-service autonomous agents. Embedding decision logic within a model using prompting strategies is brittle and lacks the modularity and control needed for real-time, multi-tool investigations.

correct_text: Use AWS Strands Agents SDK to build a custom autonomous agent, integrating SageMaker AI, Rekognition, internal APIs, and selecting a foundation model via Amazon Bedrock.
concepto: AWS Strands Agents SDK agente autonomo

category: AIP – AI Safety, Security, and Governance
stem: A healthcare organization is implementing a generative AI solution to process and analyze sensitive medical records, including patient histories and diagnostic images. The solution uses Amazon Rekognition for image analysis to extract features from diagnostic images and Amazon Textract for extracting text from scanned medical forms. The organization must ensure that only authorized users and services have access to specific subsets of sensitive medical data stored in Amazon S3, with the ability to classify sensitive datasets (e.g., patient health information, diagnostic images, billing records) using metadata. The team requires a solution that provides granular control over data access, ensuring that only authorized users and services can access specific portions of sensitive data for processing and inference. The solution must allow secure data access management, with the ability to monitor and audit all data access events to maintain privacy and security. Which solution best achieves these requirements?

options.text: Implement S3 bucket policies to enforce object-level access control for sensitive medical data, complemented by AWS KMS for data encryption at rest to ensure secure storage.
options.rationale: because S3 bucket policies are only limited to controlling access at the object level and do not provide the fine-grained access management needed for large-scale data governance. They lack the ability to enforce granular access at the table or column level, which is necessary for securely managing sensitive healthcare data across an entire data lake and ensuring compliance with privacy regulations like HIPAA.

options.text: Leverage AWS Lake Formation with LF-Tag-based to apply fine-grained access control policies, enabling comprehensive data governance with built-in auditing and encryption for compliance.
Configure AWS IAM roles and VPC endpoints to establish secure, private connectivity for accessing medical data, ensuring that only authorized services can interact with the data.
options.rationale: because, while IAM roles and VPC endpoints provide network-level access control and can restrict which services can connect to Amazon S3, they do not offer the centralized, fine-grained access control or auditing features needed to manage data access at scale. This solution primarily focuses on network security, not on managing detailed access policies across datasets, which AWS Lake Formation provides.

options.text: Utilize AWS Secrets Manager to securely manage API keys and credentials, while implementing access controls to ensure compliant, secure interactions with sensitive data.
options.rationale: because AWS Secrets Manager is designed to securely store and manage API keys, credentials, and other secrets, but it does not provide the fine-grained access control needed for managing large datasets, especially in a data lake environment. While it can protect access credentials, it just lacks the comprehensive data governance and access control features, such as role-based permissions and auditing, required for managing sensitive healthcare data across multiple services.

correct_text: Leverage AWS Lake Formation with LF-Tag-based to apply fine-grained access control policies, enabling comprehensive data governance with built-in auditing and encryption for compliance.
concepto: Lake Formation LF-Tag control granular para datos sensibles

category: AIP – Implementation and Integration
stem: A biotech company has developed a custom Meta Llama model to help scientists generate research summaries from large genomic datasets. The model was trained and fine-tuned using Amazon SageMaker AI, and the resulting weights were exported in Hugging Face format with .safetensors files. All model artifacts, including configuration files and tokenizer data, are stored securely in Amazon S3. The company wants to deploy this model in Amazon Bedrock for production use, providing scientists with a responsive AI assistant. The workload is predictable, and the organization wants to avoid managing underlying infrastructure while ensuring low-latency, high-throughput inference that supports multiple simultaneous requests. Which solution will best meet these requirements?

options.text: Convert the model to ONNX format and deploy it on Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling Groups with a load balancer to handle traffic spikes.
options.rationale: . This approach primarily addresses scalability through EC2 instances and load balancers, but it requires full infrastructure management, including patching, monitoring, and scaling policies. It only provides flexibility at the infrastructure level and does not leverage Bedrock’s fully managed custom model deployment capabilities. For high-throughput, low-latency inference in a production environment, this option is operationally intensive and less efficient.

options.text: Import the Hugging Face–format model files from S3 using Bedrock Custom Model Import. Deploy the model using on-demand inference for flexible, pay-per-use deployments.
options.rationale: . On-demand inference is designed for unpredictable workloads and provides pay-per-use flexibility. It simply cannot guarantee consistent low-latency performance under heavy concurrent requests. In this scenario, where multiple scientists need responsive AI outputs simultaneously, on-demand inference may lead to variable response times, making it less suitable than provisioned throughput.

options.text: Use Bedrock Custom Model Import to import the Hugging Face–format .safetensors Llama model from S3. Deploy it with Bedrock Provisioned Throughput to ensure consistent, low-latency inference at scale.
Import the fine-tuned Llama model into SageMaker Serverless Inference to provide automatically scaling, pay-per-use inference for fluctuating workloads.
options.rationale: . SageMaker Serverless Inference typically handles sporadic or fluctuating traffic without requiring server management. However, it only provides elastic scaling and does not ensure predictable, low-latency performance for high-volume inference. For workloads like genomic research, where multiple requests occur concurrently and consistently, serverless inference is less reliable compared with Bedrock Provisioned Throughput.

correct_text: Use Bedrock Custom Model Import to import the Hugging Face–format .safetensors Llama model from S3. Deploy it with Bedrock Provisioned Throughput to ensure consistent, low-latency inference at scale.
concepto: Bedrock Custom Model Import + Provisioned Throughput

category: AIP – Foundation Model Integration, Data Management, and Compliance
stem: A regional compliance oversight bureau is developing an AI-driven assistant to streamline policy interpretation and regulatory review workflows. The bureau must integrate several knowledge bases, including internal regulatory guidance, historical enforcement summaries, and department-maintained compliance wikis containing frequently updated rule interpretations. The goal is to have a consistent access layer for all content, minimal manual maintenance, and the ability for the AI assistant to reference the most current information at all times. Which of the following should be implemented?

options.text: Use AWS DataSync to periodically transfer document sets to a centralized Amazon S3 bucket and configure Amazon EMR to process and restructure the content for searchability. Maintain cron-based job definitions to ensure each source is re-copied and re-processed on a fixed interval.
options.rationale: because it depends on batch transfers and manual scheduling, which only increases operational overhead and does not provide a unified, AI-ready access layer with automated synchronization.

options.text: Unify access to all repositories using Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases. Configure data source connectors for each knowledge base and compliance wiki, and enable automated synchronization so content remains updated.

Implement a multi-source data integration approach using Amazon AppFlow for SaaS-based repositories and AWS Transfer Family for file-based sources, feed all collected data into Amazon OpenSearch Service, and coordinate recurring data refreshes with AWS Step Functions workflows.
options.rationale: because it requires multiple services stitched together with custom orchestration, which typically leads to complexity and higher maintenance. While it enables search, it lacks a native AI-ready knowledge base and introduces synchronization challenges.

options.text: Use Amazon Neptune as a central knowledge graph and develop ingestion scripts to convert all knowledge bases and compliance wikis into graph-compatible formats. Schedule batch updates to keep the datasets synchronized.
options.rationale: because it demands custom data modeling and ingestion, relies on batch updates, and is not optimized for retrieval-augmented generation or automated synchronization across diverse sources.

correct_text: Unify access to all repositories using Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases. Configure data source connectors for each knowledge base and compliance wiki, and enable automated synchronization so content remains updated.
concepto: Bedrock Knowledge Bases data source connectors + sync

category: AIP – Implementation and Integration
stem: A software-as-a-service (SaaS) company is building a personalized cabin-upgrade recommendation system powered by Amazon SageMaker AI for a travel management platform. The system is designed to help airline partners identify and target eligible passengers with tailored upgrade offers based on individual travel behavior. Models developed and trained in SageMaker AI will be imported using the Amazon Bedrock Custom Model Import feature, allowing the company to utilize Bedrock’s native inference and content safety capabilities. Passenger travel history, including previous bookings, seat preferences, and loyalty status, is stored in an Amazon RDS database and must be queried to generate personalized recommendations. The system is expected to provide accurate, consistent, and contextually relevant upgrade suggestions for all supported airline partners and passenger segments. Which approach fulfills these requirements?

options.text: Provision an Amazon DynamoDB table to cache and serve frequently accessed passenger travel records for low-latency retrieval. Use an AWS Lambda function to transform cached records into structured prompts and pass them to the recommendation model. Apply Bedrock Guardrails to filter model outputs. Use AWS Step Functions to orchestrate the end-to-end recommendation pipeline and reduce hallucinations.
options.rationale: because Amazon DynamoDB is primarily a fully managed NoSQL database service designed for high-throughput, low-latency key-value and document workloads. It is not a relational data store and does not support the structured SQL querying required to accurately retrieve passenger booking records, seat class history, and loyalty membership details from the existing Amazon RDS database. AWS Lambda is a serverless compute service used to run event-driven functions and custom business logic. Using it to manually transform cached records into prompts bypasses the precision of text-to-SQL transformations and introduces inconsistency in how passenger data is surfaced to the model. AWS Step Functions is a workflow orchestration service and is not a native mechanism for suppressing hallucinations in model outputs.

options.text: Configure text-to-SQL transformations supported by SQL validation checks to accurately extract passenger booking records, seat class history, and loyalty membership details from the RDS database. Supply the structured results to the cabin upgrade recommendation model imported via Bedrock Custom Model Import to generate targeted offers for each passenger profile. Enforce content safety on all model responses using Bedrock Guardrails. Integrate AWS Step Functions and AWS Lambda functions to execute a post-inference validation workflow and suppress hallucinations.
options.rationale: because while text-to-SQL transformations with SQL validation checks and Amazon Bedrock Custom Model Import are both appropriate components for this use case, this option relies on AWS Step Functions and AWS Lambda functions for hallucination suppression. AWS Step Functions is a serverless orchestration service used to coordinate multi-step automated workflows, and AWS Lambda executes custom serverless logic, neither is a native mechanism for evaluating the semantic relevance or factual confidence of a model’s generated output.

options.text: Ingest passenger travel history from the RDS database into an S3 data lake using AWS Glue ETL jobs. Use Amazon Athena to run scheduled queries that materialize passenger features for the recommendation model at inference time. Apply Bedrock Guardrails to filter responses. Use AWS Step Functions to orchestrate the retrieval and inference pipeline and reduce hallucinations.

Configure text-to-SQL transformations supported by SQL validation checks to accurately extract passenger booking records, seat class history, and loyalty membership details from the RDS database. Supply the structured results to the cabin upgrade recommendation model imported via Bedrock Custom Model Import to generate targeted offers for each passenger profile. Enforce content safety on all model responses using Bedrock Guardrails. Apply confidence scoring and semantic similarity searches to measure output relevance and reduce hallucinations.

correct_text: Configure text-to-SQL transformations supported by SQL validation checks to accurately extract passenger booking records, seat class history, and loyalty membership details from the RDS database. Supply the structured results to the cabin upgrade recommendation model imported via Bedrock Custom Model Import to generate targeted offers for each passenger profile. Enforce content safety on all model responses using Bedrock Guardrails. Apply confidence scoring and semantic similarity searches to measure output relevance and reduce hallucinations.
concepto: Text-to-SQL + Custom Model Import + Guardrails

stem: A large company is developing a real-time generative AI assistant to help contact center agents respond to customers during claims and policy inquiries. The application must transcribe live customer speech and begin analyzing partial conversation context before the customer finishes speaking so agents can receive suggestions as quickly as possible. The company must minimize end-to-end latency from incoming speech to the first generated suggestion displayed on the agent’s screen. The solution must use managed AWS services and support bidirectional streaming so transcription fragments and generated response updates can flow continuously during an active call. Which solution will provide the required real-time performance and streaming capabilities?

options.text: Stream the customer audio to Amazon Transcribe, but wait for each transcription segment to be finalized before sending the text to Amazon Bedrock with the InvokeModel API. Return the completed model response to the agent application through an Amazon API Gateway REST API.
options.rationale: because it typically introduces delay at multiple stages. Waiting for finalized transcription segments prevents the application from processing interim speech, while InvokeModel returns a completed response instead of streaming generated output. A REST request-response pattern also does not provide the persistent two-way connection required for continuously pushing incremental updates to agents.

options.text: Enable partial-result streaming in Amazon Transcribe so interim speech-to-text segments are available while the customer is still talking. Send the transcript fragments to Amazon Bedrock with the InvokeModelWithResponseStream API, then deliver the streamed model output to contact center agents through an Amazon API Gateway WebSocket API.

Send the live audio to Amazon Transcribe with partial results enabled and write each transcript fragment to Amazon Kinesis Data Streams. Use AWS Lambda to batch the fragments, invoke Amazon Bedrock after enough context has accumulated, and return the generated response through an Amazon API Gateway WebSocket API.
options.rationale: because batching transcript fragments would primarily delay when model inference begins. Although Kinesis and Lambda can process streaming workloads, deliberately accumulating multiple fragments before invoking Amazon Bedrock conflicts with the requirement to minimize the time from speech input to the first generated suggestion.

options.text: Use Amazon Transcribe streaming with partial results enabled and send each transcript fragment to Amazon Bedrock by using the InvokeModelWithResponseStream API. Buffer all generated response chunks in AWS Lambda and send the completed response to agents through an Amazon API Gateway WebSocket API.
options.rationale: because buffering the model output would simply remove the latency advantage of response streaming. InvokeModelWithResponseStream is designed to expose generated chunks as they become available, and API Gateway WebSocket APIs allow backend services to send messages to connected clients without waiting for the complete model response.

correct_text: Enable partial-result streaming in Amazon Transcribe so interim speech-to-text segments are available while the customer is still talking. Send the transcript fragments to Amazon Bedrock with the InvokeModelWithResponseStream API, then deliver the streamed model output to contact center agents through an Amazon API Gateway WebSocket API.
concepto: Transcribe streaming + InvokeModelWithResponseStream + WebSocket
